It captured City’s swagger, their sense of responding to what they regard as an injustice – that they maintain will be overturned on appeal – the sense they are going to continue to create an almighty headache for the Premier League. In a sea of uncertainty as to what will now happen, that is something we can be sure of.

“Cheats,” loudly boomed around Anfield from the home fans before the PA played Fleetwood Mac’s Tell Me Lies at the final whistle, as the players walked off. Those signs of defiance were not matched on the pitch. Although it may be a song City will get used to hearing for the rest of this extraordinary, unprecedented campaign.

Enzo Maresca hailed Manchester City’s ability to “make our own noise” after their emphatic 3-0 win at Liverpool.

In the first fixture since being found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges laid against them for serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, City made their statement on the pitch as they re-established a three-point lead at the top of the table.

“It was not easy for the players after the last two, three weeks, but they dealt with it very well,” Maresca, the head coach, said. “I said during the week we need to learn to deal with the outside noise because of the situation, because that will be there. But we have to make our own noise.

“Zero-three at Anfield away is a great result, for sure. I think all the organisation needs a win like this. It’s good for all [of] the club.”

Maresca said City will have to get used to such hostile occasions, with Liverpool fans making clear their anger over the judgment, and added: “All the away games are going to be with noise.”

Maresca confirmed that chief executive Ferran Soriano and director of football Hugo Viana had travelled on the team bus to Anfield in a sign of unity.

“Ferran was there, Hugo was there. We were all together,” Maresca said. “For the importance of the game, Liverpool away, Anfield away. It’s good to be together.”

The Italian claimed that despite the verdict, and the attention and uncertainty as to what will happen next, it had not affected his squad.

“The players just focus on the football. They are not thinking about the future,” he said. “It’s how we learn to deal with the noise. It’s our duty to make noise and to do that we win games. You cannot imagine how happy I am. Hopefully I am going to speak about this situation when we are going to win the appeal.”

The Liverpool boss told BBC MOTD: “I think the first part is that we played two different games. One until the red card, and then after. For 60 minutes, the players were very good. The second game from the red card was where City were better than us.

“The first yellow card was just a kick in the toe. It was nothing. It was a normal foul. It was the moment when we were pushing more. The momentum was coming for us and the atmosphere in the stadium was so nice. We conceded very little in the first half. We did a really good job. The second half, we were translating into chances.

“You learn a lot in games like today. I am very proud of my players. They put the work rate and everything in today. It’s a loss and we didn’t get anything from the performance but I liked it a lot.”

The current City players found themselves in a peculiar situation as none of this is their fault, but they’ll be the ones who receive the brunt of abuse from rival fans as the public-facing figures of the club. They’ll need to be braced for a hostile reception at every away ground in England.

However, you can expect Anfield to turn up the heat to one of the highest levels, given how alleged City’s actions have impacted Liverpool’s trophy haul.

Jurgen Klopp’s Liverpool finished second in the 2018-19 season, accumulating a staggering 98 points, while winning 30 matches and losing just once. City incredibly pipped them to the Premier League trophy by one point. A strikingly similar scenario occurred in the 2021-22 campaign, with Liverpool placing as runners-up with 92 points. You guessed it, City had 93.

What’s done is done, and ultimately we are entering a territory of ifs, buts and maybes. However, if City’s appeal against the charges is unsuccessful and the guilty verdict is upheld, then Liverpool would have unfairly missed out on historic success and lifelong memories.

“You cheating b------s, you know what you are” is audible already.

The Opta supercomputer has spoken, awarding City a 40.7 per cent chance of winning this afternoon against Liverpool’s 34.6 per cent.

However Maresca’s men well know that conqueroring Anfield is one of football’s toughest tests. In fact, away teams have only won 12.5 per cent of all Premier League matches at Liverpool’s storied home.

“Should have made it a sham and pineapple,” the company’s official account comments.

THE CHARGES HAVE BEEN DROPPED! ... on pizza for the first 114 Liverpool fans through the door of our Great Homer Street store today tastier than a massive points deduction https://t.co/Yw81xluvrT

"I think it's very difficult for the Manchester City owners to continue in their position." Jamie Carragher on Manchester City denying financial wrongdoing and their ongoing appeal. https://t.co/1r2vnze1Eb

Outside Anfield the merchandise stalls are stocking a punchy alternative to the half-and-half scarves, with these “114 Charges: Guilty” pennants, redrawing Pep Guardiola and his players as prisoners. So far I have also seen “cheats” in the font of the Oasis logo.

News breaks that City had been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges brought by the Premier League over breaches of its financial rules.

Telegraph Sport understands that Manchester United, Liverpool, Arsenal and Tottenham Hotspur were contacted in advance of the email to the other 15 clubs.

In a letter to fans, a defiant Khaldoon Al Mubarak, City’s chairman, expresses complete confidence that his club would be vindicated.

“There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club,” he writes. “We will not give them that opportunity.”

With the football world still making sense of the news, Tony Pulis admits to feeling “cheated”. His Stoke City side were defeated by Manchester City in the 2011 FA Cup final, during the 2009-23 period.

Hull City owner Acun Ilicali then likens City’s transgressions to “doping” before Mauricio Pochettino, whose Spurs side were often in the hunt with City for major trophies during his time as manager, says that football has “lived through a period of deception”.

The Premier League reveals that City’s owners inflated “sham” sponsorship deals by £830.69m between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

It also discloses that image rights had been inflated and key witnesses had lied.

Ferran Soriano, chief executive of City Football Group, appears helpless when questioned about the verdict’s findings at the European Football Clubs’ general assembly in Copenhagen by Sky News.

An unblinking Soriano then features in a video statement published by City in which he claimed their guilty verdict was based on “a single false accusation”.

With City on the ropes, Pep Guardiola releases a statement in support of his former club, assuring supporters that “we will get through this together”.

The Prime Minister says that he would be “really concerned” to lose City’s owners, but after significant backlash, No 10 moves to clarify his reaction saying that “if wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences”.

It later amends the statement to “wherever wrongdoing is established”.

The UAE then warns Andy Burnham that it will pull billions of pounds of investment out of the UK in retaliation for the guilty verdict against City.

City argue that their sponsorship deals were part-funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club’s owners, in their appeal, which claims bank statements and witness accounts provide “irrefutable evidence” to support their case.

The Liverpool head coach was asked for his reaction to City’s guilty verdict in his pre-match press conference and, as with many of his peers, he kept his response brief.

“Uncertainty is not good for anyone involved,” he said. “But there is the process ongoing and we have to be patient like everyone else and see what happens at the end.”

It is the most unlikely Oasis song title for a banner but, in a sea of canvas, the word will jump out from the Kop: Acquiesce.

The simplest flags frequently carry the most profound messages and, on a red background, below Acquiesce is the declaration: “MCFC Cheats”. It has been prepared specially and specifically for the return of domestic football to Anfield.

Given the tone coming out of the Etihad Stadium, nobody will be acquiescing to any alleged wrongdoing, certainly not on Sunday, but minds were made up on Merseyside about how far City had pushed the boundaries in pursuit of success a long time ago.

“There has been a lot of talk about various things,” explains John Gibbons, host of Anfield Wrap, the popular Liverpool podcast. “Manchester City trying to say they are going to be hard done to, but there are no great surprises among Liverpool fans about these charges, are there?

“Everyone who goes to the match, who supports Liverpool, have known all along that a lot of those sponsorship deals looked questionable. Did they pass the smell test? That’s why the atmospheres in the past when City came were always brilliant and I’m expecting it will be the same again.”

So that is why Anfield will be a maelstrom of sound and fury for one of the most significant occasions in Premier League history.

The half-and-half scarves have been replaced by more topical match-day merchandise this afternoon...

Here is what City’s head coach said during his first press conference after the guilty verdict:

“There is a process ongoing and in this moment I completely trust the club … I trust the club because I trust the people and this is also the reason why I joined the club. And then there is not another club in the world where I would [rather] be.”

“Absolutely not. The last time I was here was the treble season. I know the effort from the players, from the club, from the manager in that time that was Pep [Guardiola]. I know exactly the effort that the club put to achieve that kind of target.”

“I won the Championship with Leicester. League One, we will see, but we are thinking about something that we don’t know.”

I’m not worried at all. The environment [among] the players is nice. In this moment we are top of the league so the players have all the reason to be happy and excited.

“One hundred per cent… Because I know the organisation from years ago, and I know how serious they are, I know that they do the right things. I would like to speak about this when we win the appeal.”

While Liverpool have struggled for wins in this fixture of late, it’s worth noting that this run includes five draws.

On Saturday Manchester United fans resurrected their “ticker” mocking Manchester City’s trophy drought following their rivals’ cheating scandal:

There was also a nod to Rui Pinto, the whistleblower whose Football Leaks documents prompted the Premier League’s investigation into City:

There were four days between the news leaking that Manchester City had been found guilty of the majority of charges first levelled at them by the Premier League in February 2023 and the independent commission findings dropping.

Staff, then, had had a bit of time to process a guilty verdict although little, it seems, could adequately prepare them for the excoriating tone and content of the commission’s ruling.

“The thing that has shocked me more than anything is the language the commission used to describe the club’s conduct,” one staff member told Telegraph Sport this week.

“We had been waiting for a very long time to see what came out of these Premier League charges and lots of different things go through your head. But I just wasn’t expecting that. I’m still a bit shell-shocked by the ferocity of what the commission said. I think that’s what’s worried me.”

"Enjoy the ride and smile" Erling Haaland with a message for Man City fans ahead of their trip to Anfield this weekend 🎙️🩵 https://t.co/H7so0fk6XE

“The international break is good because we can review what we have done and what we can do better,” Enzo Maresca said after Manchester City’s harum-scarum 5-3 victory over Sunderland. “But at the same time we can relax a little bit more.” One wonders how much respite Enzo Maresca and Manchester City actually enjoyed in the intervening 21 days.

Since City last kicked a football in anger, they have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges levelled at them by the Premier League in a verdict that has shaken professional football to its very core. The club have appealed and the extent of their punishment now rests with an independent panel. Until then, though, the show goes on and City’s players and staff must compete knowing that their every move now comes with a caveat.

City have put up a united front and on Thursday Maresca and Haaland duly delivered the party lines, the City head coach revealing that the feeling among his charges was “fantastic”. “[My players] know what we can control is the football side – they are not worried at all about different things,” Maresca said, before adding that he trusts the club “completely”. The Italian doubled down on his remarks in his Friday press conference.

City maintain their innocence and many of Maresca’s peers have remained tight-lipped on the case, though Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick admitted this week he has questions, while Régis Le Bris urged football’s governing bodies to be “relentless” in safeguarding competitive integrity.

Given all that has happened, it would be easy to forget that this is, for now, a top-of-the-table clash and has been one of the Premier League’s marquee rivalries since the days of Guardiola-Jürgen Klopp. Liverpool fans have never been ones to roll out the red carpet when City are in town, but the ill feeling and belligerence will only intensify at Anfield this time around owing to the events of the past weeks.

City are top of the league having won all five of their league matches so far, while Liverpool have huffed and puffed to sixth, remaining unbeaten.

#1409. Ex-Tottenham Hotspur and Newcastle United star Sebastien Bassong is fined for dodging £7 Tube fare by using someone else's travelcard

Published: 13:02 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 16:13 EDT, 2 November 2026

Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Sebastien Bassong has been fined for dodging a £7 Tube fare after he was caught using someone else's train driver pass illegally.

The Frenchman, 40, who spent several seasons in the Premier League with Spurs, Newcastle and Norwich, was stopped by a Transport for London (TfL) officer after he was spotted tailgating a friend through the barriers at St Paul's station in May.

The ex-footballer was carrying the Oystercard of the friend's ex-girlfriend, which had been issued to her as a driver on the Docklands Light Railway (DLR), court documents showed.

The TfL officer was then told that Bassong, who was an £8 million signing for Spurs in 2009, had been using her travelcard because he was 'experiencing financial and personal hardship due to a divorce and unemployment'.

Bassong was convicted of using the rail network without a valid ticket at Wimbledon Magistrates Court on October 30.

Magistrate Graham Burbage fined him £220, ordered him to pay the £7 fare for his journey from Arnos Grove to St Paul's, and directed him to pay £250 in prosecution costs and an £88 victim surcharge.

Bassong did not enter a plea to the charge, and was convicted behind closed doors in a Single Justice Procedure hearing.

Adebukola Anifowose, a revenue control officer for TfL, told the court in a statement she spotted Bassong at 1.08pm 'pretend to tap an Oystercard enclosed in a white wallet before tailgating through the wide-aisle gate behind another male'.

Sebastien Bassong in action during a Premier League match between Chelsea and Tottenham at Stamford Bridge in 2009

Bassong attended the 2026 PFA Awards at the Manchester Opera House

The star playing for Spurs during the UEFA Champions League  match between BSC Young Boys and Tottenham Hotspur in 2010

She said Bassong offered up a TfL staff nominee pass when challenged, which allows free travel on London transport.

'System checks later confirmed that the pass did not belong to him and had last been used in October 2025,' she said.

'The accompanying male was spoken to – this individual later informed me that he was assisting Mr Bassong, who was experiencing financial and personal hardship due to a divorce and unemployment, by providing him with the nominee pass.

'It was subsequently established that the pass was registered to an ex-girlfriend of this male, who reportedly claimed to be a DLR driver.'

A notice about the prosecution was sent to Bassong's north London home, and he did not respond before the court hearing.

Bassong, who now runs a motivational coaching business, has been given 28 days to settle the court bill totalling £565.

#1408. Subcycle videography of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Strong light fields have unlocked entirely new possibilities to tailor coherent electron trajectories, engineer band structures and shape emergent phases of matter all-optically1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9. Unravelling the underlying quantum mechanisms requires a visualization of the lightwave-driven electron motion10,11 directly in the band structure. Although photoelectron momentum microscopy has imaged photoexcited electrons averaged over many cycles of light12,13,14,15,16,17,18,19, subcycle band-structure videography has been limited to small electron momenta8,20. Yet, lightwave-driven elementary processes in quantum materials often occur throughout momentum space. Here we introduce attosecond-precision, subcycle band-structure videography covering the entire first Brillouin zone and visualize one of the most fundamental but elusive strong-field processes: non-adiabatic Landau–Zener–Majorana tunnelling. The interplay of strong-field-driven acceleration within the Dirac-like band structure of graphene and periodic Landau–Zener–Majorana interband tunnelling manifests in a coherent subcycle displacement and distortion of the carrier distribution at the Brillouin zone edge. The extremely non-thermal electron distributions also allow us to disentangle competing scattering processes and assess their impact on coherent electronic control. Our panoramic view of field-driven electron motion enables a new quality of microscopic understanding of strong-field control of quantum materials.

According to the adiabatic theorem, a time-dependent, two-level quantum system remains in its ground state during a slow evolution21. By contrast, driving the system faster than its intrinsic timescale through an avoided energy crossing can create a finite occupation of the excited state by means of non-adiabatic transitions called Landau–Zener–Majorana (LZM) tunnelling22,23,24. This mechanism is central for strong-field light–matter interaction7,10,25,26. Yet, a direct observation of this foundational quantum effect in momentum space is still missing. The unique properties of graphene27 form the ideal test bed for observing LZM transitions. Its quasirelativistic electron dispersion and the robustness under irradiation with intense light have made this material a prime test ground for lightwave electronics26,28, including the demonstration of the first lightwave electronic logic gates7 and Floquet–Bloch states18,19. This has opened revolutionary prospects for quantum control, quantum sensing and quantum computation applications10,11,29.

Understanding and shaping the opportunities offered by lightwave control of electrons requires a direct observation of how LZM transitions dictate strong-field light–matter interaction. Attosecond spectroscopy has reached sufficient temporal resolution to access these dynamics30,31, and time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (trARPES) in combination with momentum microscopy32 has visualized electron dynamics directly in the band structure of quantum materials or in the orbitals of molecular layers12,13,14,15,16,17,18,19,33. trARPES with subcycle temporal resolution8,20 has combined these approaches but offered only limited 1D momentum space access. To track coherent strong-field phenomena and scattering-induced momentum redistribution, observing carrier dynamics across the entire momentum space is imperative.

Here we expand subcycle band-structure videography to the entire first Brillouin zone (BZ). The new platform overcomes previous restrictions of momentum microscopy and subcycle ARPES, increasing the momentum area accessible with subcycle resolution by more than two orders of magnitude and the available field strengths by one order of magnitude. Exploiting few-cycle mid-infrared (MIR) field transients with large peak amplitudes, we drive coherent electron dynamics at the BZ edge of graphene. This approach reveals the simultaneous displacement and distortion of the light-driven electron distribution, uncovering the interplay between coherent intraband and interband dynamics underlying LZM transitions in graphene. Moreover, tracking the non-thermal subcycle distributions in 2D momentum space reveals how different scattering processes affect lightwave-driven dynamics.

When low-intensity, short-wavelength light interacts with electrons in a solid, it can induce perturbative interband quantum jumps in momentum regions in which the occupied and unoccupied bands are separated by an integer multiple of the photon energy (Fig. 1a). In graphene, the non-trivial pseudospin texture influences the dipole moments between the lower and upper halves of the Dirac cone, leading to a distribution of excited carriers only along the direction orthogonal to the light field34,35. Conversely, a strong low-frequency field transient can adiabatically accelerate carriers within their bands on subcycle timescales, deflecting the Fermi surface in momentum space according to Bloch’s acceleration theorem (Fig. 1b). During their excursion, electrons experience an energy gap, which, in graphene, varies linearly near the K point to form an avoided crossing. Thus, field-driven acceleration may drive prototypical LZM transitions, which leave a markedly different occupation in momentum space compared with Fig. 1a. If the driving field is periodic, the phase accumulated between consecutive non-adiabatic events—the Stückelberg phase—results in so-called Landau–Zener–Stückelberg–Majorana (LZSM) interference36,37.

a, Illustration of the fundamental electronic processes governing light–matter interaction in undoped graphene at the K point in the weak-field regime. Here electrons can be promoted from the valence band to the conduction band by absorption. In graphene, the optical selection rules favour transitions in the momentum direction perpendicular to the polarization of the electric field. b, In the strong-field regime, electrons can undergo ballistic acceleration by an electric field (dashed blue arrow). Simultaneously, the field can drive interband LZM transitions on subcycle timescales, allowing electrons to tunnel from the valence band to the conduction band (solid red arrows). This results in an elongated electron distribution in the previously unoccupied conduction band, with the weight of the electron population in the direction parallel to the field. c, In the experimental scheme shown in the bottom half, an s-polarized, phase-stable MIR pulse (red) drives a monolayer of graphene, and a p-polarized XUV probe pulse (purple) at variable time delay, t, provides snapshots of the induced dynamics with subcycle temporal resolution. The photoemitted electrons (blue) enter a photoemission momentum microscope. This enables the simultaneous detection of both parallel momenta, kx and ky, and kinetic energy for every individual electron. The upper half shows a femtosecond snapshot of the 2D band structure of a monolayer of graphene, recorded with the momentum microscope. The field of view extends over the entire first BZ, allowing tracking of the electronic occupation to slightly beyond the six K points.

To access this regime, we drive electrons in epitaxially grown monolayer graphene on SiC (ref. 38) with intense phase-stable MIR pulses (central frequency, 30 THz). After a delay time, t, extreme ultraviolet (XUV) pulses (central photon energy, 21.7 eV) photoemit the electrons with subcycle resolution. Their energies and momenta are detected with a time-of-flight photoemission momentum microscope (Fig. 1c and Methods). In equilibrium, the photoemission signal maps the occupied band structure. The high XUV photon energy and the large acceptance angle of the momentum microscope capture the electronic structural dynamics throughout the entire first BZ, including its six corners, in a single measurement with sub-10-fs resolution.

Figure 2a shows several momentum distribution maps in the vicinity of a K point at selected energies. The in-plane component of the p-polarized XUV radiation driving the photoemission process is set parallel to the kx-axis. Owing to the matrix elements in the photoemission process, the intensity exhibits the characteristic horseshoe-like distribution for energies far below the Dirac point39. The influence of the dark corridor at ky = 0 and positive kx − K values is suppressed for energies close to the Dirac point, ED, and the photoemission intensity forms a disc. To ensure that the relevant dynamics occur along a direction in which the two branches of the Dirac cone have equal photoemission intensities, we apply an s-polarized MIR field along the ky-axis. For large negative delays (t = −70 fs), a slice of the photoelectron intensity for kx − K = 0 (Fig. 2b) shows two linear bands with a slope of ħvF (with the Fermi velocity vF = 10.7 Å fs−1) and a Fermi level located 200 meV above the Dirac point. With increasing t, we observe an apparent shift of the overall band structure owing to momentum streaking20 of photoemitted electrons in vacuo by the MIR field. This effect can be used to retrieve the MIR waveform at the sample surface (Extended Data Fig. 2a and Methods). Compensating for this shift isolates the subcycle electron dynamics within the band structure.

a, Zoomed-in curvature-filtered (Methods) cuts through the band structure at a selected K point. The red arrow (top) indicates the MIR polarization. The dashed grey line (bottom) marks the BZ border. The solid black lines represent the integration range in momentum space used in the three panels in b. b, Streaking-compensated and curvature-filtered view into the band structure of graphene at the Dirac point before the arrival of the MIR pulse (t = −70 fs) and for selected delay times during the interaction with the MIR pulse, t = −13.6 fs and t = 6.3 fs (raw data, Extended Data Fig. 2b). The last two snapshots show how the electron distribution is accelerated along the Dirac cone away from the equilibrium Fermi level. c, Current extracted from the occupation imbalance in the photoemission maps (blue points) and MIR waveform reconstructed from the momentum streaking (red points). Dashed black lines mark the temporal positions shown in b. The lightwave-driven current is extracted by tracking the imbalance in the occupation for positive and negative momenta (red and green shaded areas) in the raw photoemission spectra (inset) and normalized on the total amount of carriers in both regions before the pulse arrives. The grey shaded area indicates the normalized population increase in the conduction band extracted from a similar measurement.

A corresponding femtosecond snapshot of the band structure for t = −13.6 fs shows a highly non-thermal lightwave-driven electron distribution (Fig. 2b). In the upper half of the Dirac cone (E − ED ≥ 0), the ky > 0 branch is occupied up to about 1 eV, whereas the ky < 0 branch is completely unoccupied. Half a cycle of the MIR carrier wave later (t = 6.3 fs), the field direction is inverted and the electron distribution is mirrored. The extreme carrier redistribution on subcycle timescales clearly proves the non-perturbative nature of the light–matter interaction. This scenario is expected for the small Keldysh parameter near the Dirac point (γ = 0.075; Methods). Still, it is notable that the few-fs timescales accessible with our experiment allow us to see lightwave-driven intraband acceleration despite the extremely fast scattering processes in graphene33,35,40,41,42,43,44,45. Asymmetric electron distributions in momentum space correspond to the excitation of an intraband current. By tracking the imbalance in the band occupation for positive and negative ky momenta (Fig. 2c, inset and Methods), we extract the lightwave-driven intraband current density and directly compare it with the MIR driving waveform (Fig. 2c). Although the current density shows a similar envelope and oscillation frequency as the MIR transient, there is a non-trivial phase shift between the two waveforms.

From Bloch’s acceleration theorem20,46, we would expect that, in the absence of decoherence, the momentum accumulated by electrons follows the integral over the MIR field, resulting in a phase shift of π/2 between the current and the field. A Fourier analysis (Methods) allows us to retrieve this phase delay with attosecond precision. Notably, the average delay of 4.9 ± 0.2 fs is much smaller than the value associated with a fully coherent evolution (8.3 fs). Simulations based on the semiconductor Bloch equations (SBEs)6 in the relaxation time approximation (Extended Data Fig. 3 and Methods) reproduce this phase shift for a mean scattering time of 9.0 ± 0.7 fs. As non-adiabatic LZM transitions rely on the coherent and unperturbed field-driven evolution of charge carriers, this sets the time and length scales relevant for lightwave electronics. Despite the short scattering time, electrons in graphene can travel almost 100 Å owing to their large velocity of vF = 10.7 Å fs−1.

Most notably, the current is accompanied by an ultrafast increase of the total conduction-band population within the strongest MIR half-cycles (Fig. 2c, grey shaded area). Perturbative interband transitions are too weak to become effective on subcycle timescales and, in equilibrium, straightforward vertical interband transitions are prohibited in the doped sample by Pauli blocking. Hence, the observed electronic structural dynamics attest to an interplay between strong-field-driven intraband and interband currents. Next, we unveil the microscopic mechanisms by imaging the full 2D momentum space. With this capability, unavailable in previous subcycle photoemission experiments8,20, we can directly target the coherent light–matter interaction regime and the subsequent relaxation dynamics.

Before the interaction with the MIR transient, the equilibrium carrier distribution in the conduction band (E − ED ≥ 0) of n-doped graphene can be approximated by a disc centred about each K point (Fig. 2a). If the electrons were solely subject to an accelerating electric field, they would, in accordance with Bloch’s acceleration theorem46, collectively move along the ky direction and we would merely expect a time-dependent centre-of-mass (COM) displacement of this disc. Although the streaking-compensated 2D momentum maps (Fig. 3a) indeed show pronounced oscillations of the COM displacement with the frequency of the strong driving field and a maximum amplitude of 0.078 Å−1 (Fig. 3b), they also reveal a further notable change of their shape (Fig. 3a,c). The observed deviations from the initial shape of the distribution are on the same order as the COM displacement.

a, Streaking-compensated 2D carrier distribution in the conduction band for selected delay times. The inset indicates the position of the evaluated window in momentum space and the arrow shows the MIR polarization. The grey lines mark the BZ borders. The Gaussian fits illustrate the width of the projection of the carrier distribution on the kx-axis (brown) and the ky-axis (green). The fits of the first panel are shown in black in the later snapshots as a reference. Under the influence of the field, the carrier distribution is displaced along ky (t = −43.6 fs). Owing to LZM transitions, the carrier distribution is elongated along ky, forming an ellipse (t = 3 fs). For later delays (t = 26.3 fs), scattering leads to a broadening also along kx. For vanishing fields, the electron distribution relaxes back to its original shape (t = 233 fs). b, Displacement of the COM of the electron distribution. The inset shows the Fourier transform of the oscillating electron distribution (green line) and the driving field (red shaded area). Dashed black lines mark the temporal positions of the momentum maps in a. c, Evolution of the change in the size of the electron distribution, Δσ, characterized by the width of the Gaussians used to fit the carrier distribution along the kx-axis (brown) and the ky-axis (green). The Fourier transform in the inset reveals oscillations in the width of the distribution along the ky-axis, with pronounced components at the second harmonic of the driving frequency during the initial half-cycles of the driving field (grey shaded area). The vertical orange lines in b and c are guides to the eye to relate the oscillation in the width of the electron distribution to the motion of its COM.

Already after the first MIR field cycles (Fig. 3a, t = 3 fs), the Fermi surface is strongly elongated from 0.054 Å−1 to 0.096 Å−1 in the direction parallel to the field, whereas the change in the orthogonal direction is only 0.014 Å−1 (Fig. 3a, Gaussian fits). The Fermi surface is no longer circular but takes on an elliptical shape. The time-dependent change in the ky width (Fig. 3c, green line) directly correlates with the field strength. Furthermore, this width oscillates at twice the MIR carrier frequency while the COM displacement tracks the electric field similarly to the current plotted in Fig. 2c. Because the maximum broadening coincides with the peak COM displacement, we can rule out motion blur as the origin of the elongation in the ky direction. Notably, the electron distribution encompasses the Dirac point at all delay times, even for the largest displacements.

All of these intriguing dynamics can be microscopically explained by a full quantum-mechanical solution of the SBEs6 (Methods), which account for intraband and interband transitions as well as LZM-type interband coupling, on equal footing. A systematic switch-off analysis pinpoints how specific aspects of coherent strong-field light–matter interaction manifest in the observed dynamics (Extended Data Fig. 4a). The periodic COM shift of the electron distribution is clearly associated with field-driven intraband motion of charge carriers. Yet, the distribution retains its circular shape and separates from the K point for large displacement if interband dynamics are switched off. Once interband coupling is included, the theory shows the same elongation of the carrier distribution as the experiment (Extended Data Fig. 4b). The theory also qualitatively reproduces the increase in carrier density in the conduction band (Extended Data Fig. 5), confirming that interband transitions at the K point act like a well that feeds electrons into the upper part of the Dirac cone on subcycle timescales.

These transitions originate from strong-field interband coupling, whereas conventional perturbative interband photoexcitation is suppressed by orders of magnitude under our experimental conditions (Extended Data Fig. 6). Owing to pseudospin selection rules34,35, photoexcitation would occur in momentum regions with |kx − K| > 0, located perpendicular to the polarization of the incident light (Extended Data Fig. 6a). By contrast, the coupled intraband and interband dynamics of the LZM scenario leads to the observed unidirectional elongation of the electron distribution parallel to the electric field (Extended Data Fig. 6b). Simulations with varying field strengths confirm that this feature is characteristic of the strong-field regime (Extended Data Fig. 7).

The region in which LZM-type tunnelling can occur is determined by the field strength, E0, and the energy gap, which increases linearly with |kx − K|. For E0 = 1.57 MV cm−1, the transition region is confined to momenta |kx − K| ≤ 0.08 Å−1 (Fig. 3a, t = 3 fs), corresponding to a Keldysh parameter of γ ≤ 0.63. Accounting for scattering and limited momentum resolution, this value is in good agreement with the original LZM formula \({P}_{{\rm{L}}{\rm{Z}}{\rm{M}}}=\exp \left(-2{\rm{\pi }}\frac{\hbar {v}_{{\rm{F}}}}{2|e|{E}_{0}}{|{k}_{x}-K|}^{2}\right)\), which predicts diabatic transitions in a momentum range |kx − K| ≤ 0.04 Å−1 (probability 1/e2 width; Methods). This confirms that the linearly dispersing Dirac cone of graphene is a perfect realization of the original model Hamiltonian23. And even Landau, Zener and Majorana’s assumption that the energy levels intersect at a constant speed holds true, as the strong driving fields propel the electrons past the intersection point in less than 1 fs—much faster than the MIR oscillation period (Methods).

The interplay between intraband motion and LZM tunnelling also explains the modulations of the width observed at twice the driving frequency (Fig. 3c). Because the region close to the K point features the lowest tunnelling barrier, electron injection into the upper part of the Dirac cone becomes most efficient in the few-fs time window between a field extremum and the nearest peak displacement of the pre-existing population, which occurs twice per optical cycle. Scattering shortens this time window, shifting the optimal injection time. This situation should result in a step-like increase of the population in the conduction band, with a phase determined by the interplay of Pauli blocking, the evolution of the field amplitude and scattering (Methods). However, a step-like increase can only be reproduced by simulations using extremely strong dephasing that destroys the quantum memory between successive LZM transitions (Extended Data Fig. 9). For realistic dephasing rates, the step-like character transforms into pronounced 2ω oscillations. Their presence in the experimental width of the electron distribution suggests interference of electrons owing to their accumulated phase between individual tunnelling events, emphasizing the role of quantum coherence in light-field-driven devices.

Although LZM dynamics dominate at early delay times, scattering limits the time frame for fully coherent light–matter interaction. At t = 26.3 fs (Fig. 3a), the initially anisotropic electron distribution broadens also along the kx direction and approaches a circular shape with a radius of about 0.065 Å−1, before it contracts to a more equilibrated and isotropic distribution (t = 233 fs). This ultrafast change of the elliptical distribution (Fig. 3c) reflects the interplay between field-driven acceleration, LZM transitions, scattering and carrier relaxation. Our SBE simulations (Extended Data Fig. 10 and Methods) predict distinctive momentum fingerprints for electron–electron and electron–optical phonon scattering. 2D mapping thus allows us to identify their signatures (Fig. 4a). Neglecting all forms of scattering results in a broadening (up to 0.053 Å−1) and displacement (about 0.107 Å−1) of the carrier density along the ky direction and the distribution remains elliptical after the MIR pulse (t = 233 fs), retaining the momentum hallmark of LZM transitions. Moreover, the phase delay of the microscopic current (Fig. 4b) is approximately π/2, as expected for undamped intraband motion. Introducing electron–electron scattering, the initially strongly broadened and displaced momentum distribution (t = 27 fs) partially thermalizes (t = 233 fs) and shrinks to a circular shape with a radius of about 0.038 Å−1. Still, the peculiar angular dependence of electron–electron scattering41,47 retains a large ellipticity on shorter timescales, and the phase delay is only marginally affected. This is caused by the reduced phase space for scattering imposed by the pseudospin texture of graphene.

a, Simulated 2D carrier density, n, in the conduction band for selected delay times with different scattering contributions. The leftmost panels show how the carrier distribution behaves for intermediate and late delay times t, based on the SBEs without scattering. The light grey line marks the half-maximum contour, highlighting the shape of the carrier distribution. For comparison, the dark grey line shows the corresponding contour when also excluding interband coupling, emphasizing its role in reproducing the experimental observations. It is included in the other panels for reference. The middle and right panels show the carrier distribution including different scattering channels: electron–electron (ee) scattering and electron–electron combined with electron–optical phonon (ee + op) scattering, respectively. The cartoons in the insets illustrate the regions in momentum space accessible for an electron (small, blue sphere) through scattering (dark regions: accessible; bright regions: inaccessible). b, Time-dependent evolution of the extracted current for different scattering mechanisms (dotted purple line: no scattering; dotted light blue line: ee scattering; solid blue line: ee + op scattering). The driving field is shown as a red line. Electron–electron scattering affects the phase delay only slightly, whereas including electron–optical phonon scattering affects it markedly. c, Temporal evolution of the change in the width of the electron distribution, Δσ, along kx (brown) and ky (green) for different levels of theory (line style as in b; dotted lines: no scattering and ee scattering; solid lines: ee + op scattering). Without scattering (dotted curves), the distribution is broadened strongly only in the direction of the field. By including scattering with optical phonons (solid curves), it is possible to reach a qualitative agreement with the experiment. a.u., arbitrary units.

Simulations including scattering with Γ point longitudinal (LO) and transverse (TO) optical phonons reproduce the experimentally observed dynamics very well. For t = 27 fs, the electron distribution shows a substantial broadening in both the ky (about 0.051 Å−1) and the kx (about 0.041 Å−1) directions, associated with an isotropic redistribution of the charge carriers. This leads to a nearly circular distribution whose COM is shifted by only 0.008 Å−1 at t = 27 fs, much less than in the previous cases. This results from a large change in the phase delay (Fig. 4b), approaching a value of π/4. After the pulse (t = 233 fs), the distribution relaxes to a fully circular shape with a radius of approximately 0.031 Å−1. Both the phase delay and the time-dependent broadening of the electron distribution (Fig. 4c) are in good qualitative agreement with the experiment. We can, thus, identify the key limiting factor for coherent control dictated by the fastest momentum redistribution channel, which, in graphene, is electron–optical phonon scattering (Fig. 4b, solid blue line).

Our experiment opens the momentum horizon of subcycle photoemission over the entire first BZ of basically any quantum material. This universal tool enabled us to directly observe LZM transitions in the band structure of a solid. Attosecond-precision videography of graphene unravels how interband LZM tunnelling couples to field-driven intraband acceleration along the Dirac cone and how scattering influences and limits a fully coherent evolution. This platform may soon address other key questions of condensed matter physics and ultrafast information technologies, from optical band-structure engineering and phase transitions to light-field-driven sculpting of molecular orbitals.

The subcycle momentum microscopy setup (Extended Data Fig. 1a) is based on two ytterbium-doped potassium gadolinium tungstate (Yb:KGW) amplifiers (CARBIDE, Light Conversion Inc.). Each amplifier generates near-infrared light pulses with a duration of 250 fs, a centre wavelength of 1,030 nm and a pulse energy of 1.5 mJ, at a repetition rate of 50 kHz. In the probe arm, the second harmonic of the output of a four-stage noncollinear optical-parametric amplifier (NOPA; ORPHEUS-OPCPA, Light Conversion Inc.)48 yields carrier-envelope phase (CEP)-stabilized pulses centred at 400 nm with a pulse duration of 20 fs. These pulses are focused into a high-pressure argon gas jet to generate high-order harmonics (Extended Data Fig. 1b) in a vacuum beamline49. The seventh harmonic at a photon energy of 21.7 eV is spectrally selected by two multilayer mirrors (Extended Data Fig. 1b, grey shaded area). They feature a bandwidth of 0.9 nm around 57 nm and thus support a Fourier-limited pulse duration of less than 10 fs. The XUV pulses enter the experimental ultrahigh-vacuum (UHV) chamber, the momentum microscope32, through a 200-nm-thin aluminium foil, which also filters out the ultraviolet driving pulses.

Because the count rate in a time-of-flight photoemission momentum microscope is limited to only about one electron per laser shot, a high repetition rate is key for keeping measurement times at a reasonable amount while ensuring good statistics. In our experiment, this requirement entails the challenge of pushing the generation of the atomically strong, few-cycle phase-stable MIR pump pulses to new limits for a tabletop setup. Here the generated phase-stable MIR pulses feature, to the best of our knowledge, record-high average powers of up to 1 W and electrical peak field strengths of more than 200 MV cm−1. These field transients are obtained by difference frequency generation in a gallium selenide crystal between the outputs of two parallel (N)OPAs (ORPHEUS-MIR, Light Conversion Inc.)50. They feature pulse durations down to sub-50 fs and can be tuned between 4 µm and 15 µm. A small portion of the laser fundamental is picked off to pump a home-built single-stage NOPA. It is optimized to generate 10-fs pulses centred around 825 nm, which are used for electro-optic sampling (EOS) of the MIR waveforms. Extended Data Fig. 1c shows a typical MIR transient detected by EOS. A pair of wire-grid polarizers allows us to precisely control the polarization direction and power of the MIR pulses, which are then coupled into the UHV chamber through a diamond window.

The intense MIR pump (s-polarized) and the XUV probe (p-polarized) are spatially overlapped in the vacuum chamber with a custom-built off-axis parabolic mirror featuring a small aperture for XUV transmission and are focused onto monolayer graphene with an angle of incidence of 70°. A piezo-controlled delay stage in the excitation beam path allows us to set the delay between the MIR and XUV pulses with a temporal precision of 230 as. The emitted photoelectrons are detected by a time-of-flight momentum microscope (lens system: GST mbH; detector: HEX40, RoentDek)51. Multihit detection ensures linearity of the signal up to a repetition rate of 20 kHz. The combination of the 21.7-eV probe pulses with the large acceptance angle of the momentum microscope allows access to momentum regions up to ±2.14 Å−1, as compared with ±0.16 Å−1 in previous subcycle ARPES experiments8,20. The energy resolution is limited by the broad spectrum of the probe pulse. The bandwidth of the XUV pulse is tunable, setting a limit for the energy resolution of 180 meV. The momentum resolution is better than 0.01 Å−1. The custom-designed UHV chamber is shielded by a μ-metal liner and maintains a base pressure of 2 × 10−10 mbar. The samples were measured at room temperature.

Inducing field-driven dynamics in the monolayer requires a field that is parallel to the plane of the monolayer. To maximize the corresponding field component, the MIR pulse is s-polarized. The polarization of the XUV pulse is set to be perpendicular to the MIR pulse to prevent crosstalk between their fields that could introduce coherent artefacts effects in the observed dynamics. Finally, the rotation of the sample is chosen such that the MIR-induced momentum streaking in vacuum is minimized at one of the K points. This requires one K point to be at k∥ = 0, with k∥ being the momentum direction parallel to the electric field of the MIR pulse. This alignment also minimizes matrix-element-induced asymmetries along k∥ = 0 in the observed energy and momentum range. Although an asymmetry along the kx direction might persist, it is rather small at the observed energies. This is because the dark corridor only begins to set in at relatively high excitation energies, which do not occur along the kx direction in the experiment. This may also explain the slightly larger broadening observed in the simulations in which the matrix element was neglected.

For sample preparation, an n-doped 6H-SiC(0001) wafer was used as a substrate for growing an epitaxial monolayer graphene with 0° rotational alignment relative to the substrate lattice (0°-EMLG). The wafer was initially degassed in UHV at 880 °C for 30 min. The temperature was subsequently increased to 1,050 °C and maintained for 30 min under an external flux of Si atoms, resulting in a Si-rich (√3 × √3)R30° surface reconstruction. The sample was then further annealed at 880 °C for an extra 30 min, again under Si flux, resulting in the Si-rich (3 × 3) surface reconstruction. With this procedure, the oxide layer is removed from the SiC surface and atomic cleanness is achieved. In the next step, 0°-EMLG was obtained by annealing the sample at 1,400 °C for 30 min in borazine (B3N3H6) atmosphere with a partial pressure of 1.5 × 10−6 mbar. The borazine molecules act as surfactants on the heated SiC surface. They inhibit the formation of the conventional 30°-rotated graphene layer but instead force the homogeneous graphene layer in an unconventional 0° orientation with respect to the substrate lattice. For more details on the preparation of the 0°-EMLG, see refs. 38,52,53. Following growth, the surface morphology and crystalline structure were characterized using low-energy electron microscopy and low-energy electron diffraction. The average width of terraces on the SiC surface is approximately 160 nm and the surface is fully covered by 0°-EMLG. Subsequently, the sample was shortly exposed to air, transported in static vacuum (0.1 mbar) to the experimental chambers and degassed at 350 °C for 3 h before the measurements. The photoemission experiments reveal that the 0°-EMLG sample is n-doped, with the Fermi level approximately 200 meV above the Dirac point.

The acceleration of photoemitted electrons in vacuum allows for an in situ reconstruction of electric field waveforms20. In addition to acceleration within the sample, the s-polarized field also accelerates electrons after they have left the material. This causes a momentum change of the entire band structure parallel to the surface of the sample, Δk∥, that follows the vector potential of the field. The electric field waveform can thus be calculated by:

To extract Δk∥, the extracted photoemission data are shifted stepwise along k∥ and compared with a reference spectrum without a field. Within a fixed momentum window centred on the Dirac point, spanning +160 meV to −1.5 eV relative to the Fermi level (a range that, at equilibrium, encompasses predominantly the valence band), the sum of absolute pixel-wise differences between the measured data and the reference is computed at each iteration. The iteration with the smallest overall error gives the value for Δk∥. Repeating this procedure for every delay point, t, allows a reconstruction of the applied field E∥(t). To refine the retrieved waveform, a second method for extracting Δk∥(t) is used. Tracking the change in the number of electrons, integrated over all detected energies (+1 eV to −7 eV), with positive or negative momentum along k∥, yields a unitless quantity directly proportional to Δk∥(t), which is not subject to discretization caused by the binning of the data along k∥. The waveform that can be extracted in this way is then scaled by the peak electric field from the first method. The resulting waveform is shown in Fig. 2c.

The extracted Δk∥ is also used to compensate for the streaking in the photoemission spectra. As well as the trivial shift along k∥, a shift in energy, Δε, is connected to momentum streaking. The energy of every electron in vacuum is given by:

The change in energy caused by Δk∥ can therefore be calculated with:

Extended Data Fig. 2a shows band-structure snapshots taken without an applied field (left panel) and with a strong field applied before streaking compensation (middle panel) and after streaking compensation (right panel). The streaking-induced changes of energy and momentum were compensated for in all photoemission spectra before further analysis of the occupation of the band structure.

A parameter that is frequently used to distinguish between the weak-field and strong-field regimes of light–matter interaction is the Keldysh parameter

It was introduced by Leonid Keldysh in 1965 as the ratio between the carrier frequency of light ω and the tunnelling rate of an electron with mass \({m}_{{\rm{e}}+{\rm{h}}}^{\ast }\) through a barrier Δ, to show that tunnelling and multiphoton ionization in strong electromagnetic fields follow essentially the same physical laws54. This ratio scales linearly with frequency ω and the inverse of the electric field strength E0. Tunnelling dominates for γ ≪ 1, which holds for sufficiently strong fields and/or low frequencies. Equivalently, it can be expressed as \(\gamma =\sqrt{\Delta /{2U}_{{\rm{P}}}}\) by comparing the barrier Δ with the mean kinetic energy of a free electron in an oscillating electric field of amplitude E0, the ponderomotive potential \({2U}_{{\rm{P}}}={e}^{2}{E}_{0}^{2}/4{m}_{e+h}^{\ast }{\omega }^{2}\). Although similar considerations can be made for quasirelativistic motion of electrons in gapless graphene, it is more realistic for the present experiment to take the full Dirac cone with its distribution of barriers and effective masses into account (Extended Data Fig. 7a). In that case, we obtain a kx-dependent Keldysh parameter26

because both the gap, Δ = 2ħvF|kx|, and the effective mass at the gap, \({m}_{e+h}^{\ast }=\hbar |{k}_{x}|/2{v}_{{\rm{F}}}\), depend on the distance from the Dirac point. By identifying Δ with the MIR photon energy of 124 meV, we get γ = 0.075 for the peak electric fields of 1.57 MV cm−1. If we could switch off intraband acceleration, the relevant transition energy from the valence band to the unperturbed conduction band would increase to two times the doping energy of 200 meV, that is, to Δ = 400 meV. Even then, γ = 0.24 would comfortably place our measurements in the strong-field regime.

The microscopic intraband current density for each time instant, j(t), is directly extracted from the individual photoemission measurements, as in Fig. 2c. After compensation of momentum streaking, the photoemission intensity is integrated in two momentum regions with ky < 0 and ky > 0, respectively, and normalized by the total number of carriers in the two momentum regions at equilibrium. Subtracting the time-dependent number of counts with positive and negative ky components, we obtain a dimensionless value proportional to the microscopic current. To reveal the maximum amplitude of the current density, this procedure is performed for all carriers above the Dirac point (E − ED ≥ 0) within the momentum region |kx − K| < 0.15 Å−1. The result is then calibrated to physical values by multiplying with the Fermi velocity and carrier density in the conduction band of graphene with a Fermi level located 200 meV above the Dirac point, which can be computed from the density of states27. This yields a maximum current density of j(t) = 38.2 A cm−1. This value is very high, as it is even larger than in previous studies on topological insulators8,20, in which the scattering times were two orders of magnitude longer. Given the higher Fermi velocity and field amplitude, a higher current could be expected in the presented experiment. Yet, in a Drude-like regime, this would not be sufficient to compensate for the much higher scattering rate. This confirms that, in ballistic regimes, the current does not follow the Drude model. The same procedure is applied to the results of the simulations based on the SBEs.

To extract the relative timing between the microscopic current in the Dirac cone, j(t), and the electric field waveform, E(t), we apply a phase delay analysis. We compute the product between the Fourier transform of the field waveform, \(\mathop{E}\limits^{ \sim }(\omega )=F\{E(t)\}\), and the complex conjugate of the Fourier transform of the current, \(\mathop{j}\limits^{ \sim }(\omega )=F\{j(t)\}\):

The squared modulus of P(ω) peaks at the frequency of the pump field, whereas its phase corresponds to the timing difference (or phase delay) between the two oscillating quantities. We thus define the average phase difference as:

in which φ[P(ω)] is the complex phase of P(ω) and summations only consider frequencies at which |P(ω)| is larger than 50% of its peak value. To compute the phase delay, τi, we need to divide this quantity by the central frequency of the pump field. We then obtain the mean phase delay, τϕ, and the associated standard deviation of the mean over repeated measurements as:

in which i = 1,…, N runs over three different measurements performed on this sample geometry.

By performing a gated phase delay analysis, it is also possible to calculate a time-dependent phase difference, ϕ(t), which indicates the evolution of the scattering processes throughout the duration of the pulse. Here, however, the delay remains relatively stable over the first 100 fs of the driving pulse. We therefore use a single average phase shift, which we associate with a characteristic scattering time. In principle, however, this method could open new avenues for investigating relaxation dynamics across different samples with unprecedented temporal resolution.

In these equations, E(t) is the MIR electric field, T2 = 5 fs is the phenomenological dephasing time of the microscopic polarization, εe(k) and εh(k) are the energy values of the conduction and valence bands and

The out-of-equilibrium dynamics shown in Extended Data Figs. 4 and 9 were simulated on a 250 × 250 2D square (kx, ky) grid in momentum space. The grid is centred on one of the K points with coordinates kx,K = 1.703 Å−1 and ky,K = 0 and it has a side length of 0.73 Å−1. The simulated time axis ranges from −100 fs to 300 fs, with a step size of 2 fs. The electric field, E(t), is parallel to ky and its temporal profile is analytically fitted to the experimentally measured field. At the initial time instant (t0 = −100 fs), we assume peh(k, t0) = 0, whereas the electron distribution corresponds to a Fermi–Dirac distribution. The position of the Fermi level compared with the Dirac crossing is set to εF = 0.2 eV to match the experiment. Simulations comparing the dynamics at other driving frequencies, varying field strengths or different Fermi levels sometimes used analytically modelled waveforms and smaller grid sizes to keep up with increased demands for spatial or temporal resolution.

In simulations including scattering, the grid was adjusted to 50 × 50 while maintaining the size in momentum space, to save resources. To reproduce the time-dependent electron distribution observed in momentum space, it is imperative to realistically model the scattering rates:

On these timescales, two physical phenomena mainly contribute to the scattering rates:

in which \({\varGamma }_{{\bf{k}},{\rm{e}}{\rm{p}}}^{\alpha }\) and \({\varGamma }_{{\bf{k}},{\rm{e}}{\rm{e}}}^{\alpha }\) are, respectively, the electron–phonon and electron–electron scattering rates.

Starting from the electron–phonon interaction, the scattering rate can be written as57:

in which v is the phonon mode considered and α, α′ ∈ {e, h} are the band indexes. The first term thus describes transitions from an occupied (k′, α′) state to an empty (k, α) state owing to the interaction with a v phonon, whereas the second term describes the opposite process. Whereas in the former the state (k, α) is empty and becomes occupied (thus, the rate is positive), in the latter, the rate must be negative. The probability of these transitions is associated with the electron–phonon transition rate:

in which \({G}_{{\alpha }^{{\prime} }\alpha }^{v}({{\bf{k}}}^{{\prime} },{\bf{k}})\) is the electron–phonon coupling constant, δ is the Kronecker delta imposing energy and momentum conservation, q and \({\omega }_{{\bf{q}}}^{v}\) are the momentum and angular frequency of a v phonon, respectively, and \({n}_{{\bf{q}}}^{v}\) is the number of v phonons with a given frequency and momentum, which is described by the Bose–Einstein distribution.

To simplify our description, we assume that: (1) Umklapp processes are negligible and (2) the number of phonons \({n}_{{\bf{q}}}^{v}\) is constant and equal to its value at equilibrium (phonon bath). Moreover, previous works explained the dominating contribution of LO and TO phonons34,47. We will thus limit our model to LO and TO phonons and, because they have similar phonon energies (\({\omega }_{{\bf{q}}}^{{\rm{LO}}}\simeq {\omega }_{{\bf{q}}}^{{\rm{TO}}}\simeq 164.6\,{\hbar }^{-1}\,{\rm{meV}}\)) and matrix elements but their angular dependencies compensate each other, we will treat them together with an effective electron–optical phonon coupling constant57:

The effective matrix element is constant in momentum space and its value is adjusted to reproduce the experimental data. Owing to the isotropic angular dependence of this term, electron–optical phonon scattering will lead to a rapid spreading of the electron distribution around the Dirac cone.

In the same spirit, the scattering rate for electron–electron interaction can be written as57:

in which \(\alpha ,{\alpha }^{{\prime} },\beta ,{\beta }^{{\prime} }\in \{{\rm{e}},{\rm{h}}\}\) are the band indices. The associated transition rate can thus be written as57:

with A = 4π2/Δk2. The screening of the Coulomb interaction is given by the dielectric function \({\epsilon }(q)=1+{v}_{{\rm{c}}}(q)D({\varepsilon }_{{\rm{F}}})\mathop{\Pi }\limits^{ \sim }(q)\)57,58, in which:

and rS is the Wigner–Seitz radius of graphene, kF = εF/(ħvF) the Fermi wavevector and D(ε) the density of states close to the Dirac point. This approximation holds for n ≥ nth = 1012 cm−2, thus if εF ≥ 37.14 meV, as in our case.

In this form, the scattering rate for electron–electron interaction is computationally extremely expensive. Therefore, we assume that the electron distribution for the second particle can be approximated by the equilibrium Fermi–Dirac distribution of the carriers:

This allows us to write a simplified expression for the electron–electron scattering rate:

in which we use that \({S}_{{\rm{ee}}}({\bf{k}},{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast },{{\bf{k}}}^{{\prime} },{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }^{{\prime} })={S}_{{\rm{ee}}}({{\bf{k}}}^{{\prime} },{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }^{{\prime} },{\bf{k}},{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast })\) and define:

In our simulations, we only focus on a small momentum space region around one of the six equivalent K points. In doing so, we neglect intervalley electron–phonon and electron–electron scattering processes, which are not expected to contribute notably in these conditions34. However, for electron–electron scattering, it is possible that an electron scatters from one state to another within the same valley by interacting with a charge carrier in a different one. For this reason, we effectively account for these processes by multiplying \({S}_{{\rm{ee}},\beta \beta {\rm{{\prime} }}}^{{\rm{eff}},1}\) and \({S}_{{\rm{ee}},\beta \beta {\rm{{\prime} }}}^{{\rm{eff}},2}\) by the number of equivalent K valleys, that is, six. To reproduce the experimental data, we assumed Veff = 4.386. It is important to notice that the dependence on the relative angle between k, k′, \({{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }\) and \({{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }^{{\prime} }\) determines the characteristic angular dependence of electron–electron scattering in graphene47, also termed collinear scattering41. Notably, at variance with the relaxation time approximation, our approach does not enforce any specific electron distribution at any time instant, while matching our experimental results.

To reduce the computational costs when relating the phase delay to an effective scattering time, a customary approach when solving the SBEs is to invoke the relaxation time approximation6,20,55,56. In this context, the scattering rate \({\varGamma }_{{\bf{k}}}^{\alpha }\) is assumed to be inversely proportional to a time constant, T1, associated with the mean free time between scattering events. Defining \({f}_{\alpha }^{(0)}({\bf{k}})\) as the equilibrium electron distribution in the α band, we obtain:

It is important to notice that, even though this approach allows us to extract an effective time constant, it is not enough to reproduce the experimental data. In fact, in this approximation, the scattering rate at a given point k in momentum space will only depend on the instantaneous electron distribution at that point and not on any other point in momentum space. This makes it impossible to reproduce any carrier redistribution dynamics in momentum space owing to, for example, the interaction with optical phonons.

The original works of Landau22, Zener23, Majorana24 and Stückelberg36 considered a two-state quantum system with an energy separation Δε = ε1(t) − ε2(t) = αt that changes linearly with time and undergoes an avoided crossing with a half gap energy δ. The diabatic transition probability is then given by26

with the diabaticity parameter \(\varGamma =\frac{{\delta }^{2}}{\hbar \alpha }\). This simple formula can be used to estimate the region in momentum space in which transitions occur in our experiment. The model is applicable under the condition that the characteristic sweep time through the transition, τ = 2δ/ε, is short compared with the oscillation period T = 2π/ω of the driving electric field. In this case, the field can be considered quasistatic during the transition and we simply have \(\alpha =2{v}_{{\rm{F}}}\hbar |{k}_{x}-K|=2{v}_{{\rm{F}}}|e|{E}_{0}\). With δ = vFħ|kx − K|, we obtain \(\tau =\frac{\hbar | {k}_{x}-K|}{|e|{E}_{0}}=\frac{\gamma }{\omega }\). Because γ ≈ 0.1, the crossing indeed occurs very fast (τ < 1 fs). For the peak electric field E0 = 1.57 MV cm−1, the diabaticity parameter \(\varGamma =\frac{\hslash {v}_{{\rm{F}}}}{2|e|{E}_{0}}{|{k}_{x}-K|}^{2}\,\cong \) \(210\,{{\rm{\mathring{\rm A} }}}^{2}{|{k}_{x}-K|}^{2}\) becomes smaller than 1/π for |kx − K| < 0.04 Å−2. In this region around the Dirac point, 1 − e−2 = 86% of the transitions from the valence band to the conductions band are expected to take place as long as Pauli blocking can be neglected. This region roughly coincides with the momentum area in which the conduction band of our doped graphene samples is occupied. This shows that transitions can only take place after the electrons have been accelerated away from the Dirac point. After several driving cycles, the observed dynamics of the doped and a hypothetical undoped sample are expected to be similar (Extended Data Fig. 8).

For an empty upper Dirac cone, we expect the carrier injection rate owing to LZM tunnelling to closely follow the magnitude of the electric field and the electron population to increase stepwise, with the highest injection rates occurring at the largest absolute field values. In an n-doped system and for high injection rates, as in the present experiment, Pauli blocking modifies this simple picture (Extended Data Fig. 5a). Electrons can only be injected when there is sufficient empty space in the conduction band near the K point. Consequently, intraband transport plays a decisive role in determining the injection timing. Carrier injection happens most efficiently during the intervals between the extrema of the electric field and the carrier displacement. Our simulations clearly show that this results in a phase delay between the population jumps and the field, which grows as more population has been transferred. Beyond the effects of Pauli blocking and scattering, the injection dynamics can be strongly influenced by quantum interference59. Here we find that they can cause a deviation of a step-like increase in the conduction band population (or electron distribution width) by transforming the plateau regions, following a strong injection phase, into local minima through destructive interference of electron wavepackets (Extended Data Fig. 9). Although the signal-to-noise ratio of the measured conduction band population does not allow us to resolve the jumps in the population during carrier injection experimentally, the dynamics of the increase of the carrier density can be well reproduced with the theory.

The simulations also show that the elongation of the conduction band electron distribution in momentum space is closely tied to the carrier population (Extended Data Fig. 5b). Notably, the weak oscillations in the width of the electron distribution, which are superimposed on the stepwise increase, become more pronounced with scattering (Fig. 4c). This effect is probably caused by a shortening of the effective injection time window. In the absence of scattering, the electron displacement follows the vector potential and is therefore phase-shifted by π/2 relative to the electric field. With scattering, the phase shift between the electric field and the displacement of the electrons shrinks, such that periods of rapid population increase occur only a few femtoseconds before an extremum in the displacement (Extended Data Fig. 5). Experimentally, the oscillation of the width of the electron distribution at twice the frequency of the driving field is clearly visible during the first three cycles of the electric field, that is, at times when there is still substantial carrier injection (Fig. 3c). The observed relative phase with respect to the electric field transient and the COM displacement agrees well with the simulations that include scattering. The data thus support the picture of a well that is periodically driven by the electric field and opened and closed by the oscillating carriers in the conduction band.

The new experimental platform presented here was developed to give direct access to strongly driven electron dynamics without relying heavily on theory or models. This philosophy also translates to data processing: our conclusions only rely on features present in the raw data. The previously described streaking compensation is the first and only step in the data analysis pipeline that is required to ensure that the observed dynamics can be attributed to processes that are happening in the solid and not the vacuum. Following that, the general strategy is that filtering is only used to remove technical noise and signals related to the matrix elements before the data are analysed or to enhance visibility in the figures. To ensure full transparency, the following contains a summary of all notable data processing steps for the presented figures.

The raw data from the delay line detector are binned with a spacing of 0.084 eV × 0.022 Å−1 × 0.022 Å−1 for the data in Fig. 1 and with a spacing of 0.084 eV × 0.011 Å−1 × 0.011 Å−1 for all other photoemission data.

The 3D data in Fig. 1c are symmetrized to remove the decrease in photoemission intensity caused by the angle of incidence of the XUV pulse.

The 2D momentum maps in Fig. 2a are obtained by integrating the 3D data within an energy window of 0.33 eV around distinct energy levels (0.25 eV, −0.25 eV, −0.75 eV, −1.25 eV, −1.75 eV). Before plotting, the data are further processed to enhance the visibility in the figure. First, a 1D simple moving average along both momentum axes (window size: 0.08 Å−1) is applied to the data four times. The filtered data are further processed by a 2D curvature filter described by equation (11) of ref. 60 with C0 = 0.2. Finally, a 2D median filter with window size 0.045 eV × 0.045 Å−1 is applied three times to clean up numerical noise.

The band structure cuts in Fig. 2b are obtained by integrating the 3D data within a momentum window of 0.08 Å−1 around kx − K = 0. Before plotting, the data are further processed to enhance the visibility in the figure. First, a 1D simple moving average along the energy and momentum axes with window sizes of 0.59 eV and 0.08 Å−1, respectively, is applied four times. The filtered data are subject to a 2D curvature filter with C0 = 0.2. Finally, a 2D median filter with window size 0.34 eV × 0.045 Å−1 is applied three times. The raw data are shown in Extended Data Fig. 2b.

The applied field transient and current in Fig. 2c are extracted from the raw data as laid out in Methods sections ‘Electric field waveform reconstruction and streaking compensation’ and ‘Current extraction and Fourier analysis of the phase delay’. Before plotting, a 4-THz high-pass filter is applied to the data to remove slowly varying offsets. The data showing the increase of the carrier population in the conduction band were acquired under almost identical experimental conditions in which special care has been taken to align the MIR polarization such that the electric field exhibits no perpendicular component leading to coherent oscillations of the integrated photoemission intensity.

The 2D momentum maps in Fig. 3a are obtained by integrating the 3D data for energies higher than 170 meV. This energy level is chosen to minimize contributions of the valence band caused by the limited energy resolution of the setup. Before extracting the COM displacement and width, a Gaussian filter with a small window size 0.02 Å−1 × 0.02 Å−1 has been applied to the 2D data. We applied the same filter to the experimental 2D data for a better comparison between experiment and theory. For the theory data, this is necessary to reduce numerical or binning artefacts. Owing to its small window size, the filter does not change or remove any of the features retrieved for data analysis.

To extract the COM motion and change of the width of the carrier distribution shown in Fig. 3b,c, the plotted 2D maps are integrated along kx and ky. For the data along ky, a Gaussian distribution with a constant offset (accounting for the background) is fitted to the integrated distribution. For the data along kx, the previously constant offset is modified with a linear decrease for growing kx values to account for the decrease in background caused by the photoemission matrix element. The mean of the extracted fit for the ky distribution is used to characterize the COM motion. Before plotting, a 15-THz high-pass filter is applied to these data to remove a slowly varying offset. The change of the standard deviation, Δσ, of the extracted fits is used to characterize the change of the width of the carrier distribution along kx and ky.

The 2D momentum maps in Fig. 4a are obtained by integrating the simulated population of the conduction band and applying a Gaussian filter with a small window size of 0.02 Å−1 × 0.02 Å−1 to the 2D data, as described above for the data shown in Fig. 3a.

The extraction of the simulated current density and change of the width of the carrier distribution shown in Fig. 4b,c follows the procedures outlined for the experimental data.
