#1332. Embattled FIFA chief Gianni Infantino 'used Trump adviser to get work permit for his undocumented Nicaraguan housekeeper'

By ISABEL BALDWIN, US ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 15:01 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 15:47 EDT, 3 November 2026

FIFA President Gianni Infantino allegedly influenced Trump administration officials to fast-track a work permit for his undocumented Nicaraguan housekeeper after she lost her legal status, according to bombshell documents.

The global soccer chief is alleged to have turned to politically-connected contacts to secure a new work permit for Yajarlin del Socorro Fernandez, 33, after the White House revoked her legal permission to work in the United States, according to documents reviewed by the Daily Mail.

The Nicaraguan-born Fernandez was reportedly employed by the soccer governing body to work as a housekeeper for the FIFA boss and his family in August 2024. Despite being on FIFA's payroll, she performed no services for the organization.

However, she reportedly continued illegally working in her role and living in the Infantino household for months after the Trump administration terminated the immigration agreement that granted her permission to stay in the United States.

Fernandez is then said to have secured a new work authorization under Kristi Noem's Department of Homeland Security following an intervention by a Trump adviser, documents show.

Infantino allegedly tapped Carlos Cordeiro, the former US Soccer chief who served as a senior World Cup adviser to Donald Trump, to orchestrate the new work permit.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino (right) reportedly enlisted the help of a Trump adviser to secure a work permit for his family's Nicaraguan housekeeper

Infantino allegedly tapped Carlos Cordeiro (pictured) to orchestrate a new work permit for Yajarlin del Socorro Fernandez

In January, Infantino reportedly asked Cordeiro, who in May 2025 was appointed to the White House's World Cup task force alongside Noem, to use his connections at the state department to smooth the path to getting Fernandez's new work visa approved, according to the documents.

Cordeiro also allegedly first helped to secure Fernandez's right to work in the US under Infantino's orders in 2024.

Fernandez was reportedly already living and working at Infantino's residence in the millionaires' row of One Thousand Museum in Miami, Florida, where David Beckham recently sold a $25million penthouse, in early 2024.

However, until May 2024, she had not yet filed or received an approved work permit and was therefore working at the residence illegally, per the documents.

During a January 2024 meeting at Infantino's home, Cordeiro, at the FIFA boss's request, is said to have instructed a subordinate to submit their own Miami rental address on Fernandez's immigration filing rather than that of the Infantino family home.

While Fernandez's work visa was initially approved, it came to an abrupt end last year when the Department of Homeland Security terminated the Humanitarian Parole Program for Cuba, Haiti, Venezuela and her native Nicaragua.

On May 30, 2025, the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to scrap the four-country scheme, which had permitted Fernandez and other Nicaraguans to secure permission to work in the US.

Fernandez's contract with FIFA was terminated in October 2025, but she was paid a three-month salary as a bonus and remained illegally working as Infantino's housekeeper for the remainder of the year, according to the documents.

Cordeiro (left) was appointed to Trump's White House's World Cup task force in 2025

Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem worked in connection with the task force

In January 2026, Infantino allegedly asked Cordeiro, who was now working on the World Cup task force which operated directly out of Homeland Security, to leverage his new government contacts to secure Fernandez a new permit.

That same month, Fernandez was granted a new work visa and was re-hired as a FIFA employee on a $40,000-per-year contract until August.

FIFA strongly denied the allegations that it had 'employed an individual in the US without the necessary authorisation.'

'FIFA verifies the employment status of each employee and ensures compliance with U.S. immigration and employment requirements,' a FIFA spokesperson told The Daily Mail.

'Matters related to the FIFA President's personal and home life are private; however, for the avoidance of any doubt, the costs of any domestic staff are met by the FIFA President personally.

The organization added: 'As FIFA stated in August, it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine FIFA and its President. FIFA welcomes legitimate scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a license to amplify false allegations. Where reporting is inaccurate or misleading FIFA will continue to challenge it directly and vigorously.'

Cordeiro did not immediately respond to The Daily Mail's requests for comment.

The Daily Mail also reached out to the DHS for comment and to question why Fernandez was granted a new work permit but did not receive an immediate response.

Infantino, who is standing for reelection in 2027, has faced months of scrutiny

The bombshell report comes after months of scrutiny for Infantino, who faces reelection in 2027.

Infantino faced mutiny earlier this year over his secret plans – later scrapped – to sell a stake in the World Cup to private equity investors including Joshua Kushner, the brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

It sparked uncertainty around Infantino's future after three confederations rejected his plan, which was then abandoned.

Among them was UEFA, which said it has lost confidence in Infantino and threatened to boycott future World Cups.

Cordeiro also recently quit FIFA over Infantino's commercial deals with Josh Kushner's Thrive Capital.

Infantino faced further scrutiny last month when it was alleged that Infantino personally intervened to suspend USA Folarin Balogun's World Cup red card following a call with President Trump.

In a saga that sparked condemnation from across the world, the striker was originally barred from the USA's last-16 match against Belgium, only for his ban to be sensationally suspended by the FIFA disciplinary committee following a protest by the White House. The New York Post claimed in October that Infantino told Trump in a call on July 1 that 'he would take care of it. One call and it was done.'

FIFA did not comment on the claims at the time but pointed to a July statement from Infantino, when he insisted the decision was made by 'independent' bodies acting 'autonomously.'

Despite mounting pressure over recent months, Infantino intends to stand for a fourth consecutive term next March at the FIFA Congress.

Chelsea, Arsenal and Tottenham Hotspur are reportedly interested in signing AC Monza striker Gustavo Varela after his impressive Serie A performances have attracted attention from several European clubs.

According to a report from Fussball News, the three Premier League clubs have been monitoring the 21-year-old Portuguese forward, who has emerged as one of the most exciting young goalscorers in Italian football.

The 21-year-old has enjoyed a remarkable start to life at Monza since arriving from Benfica in July 2026. He has already scored nine goals in his first nine Serie A appearances, establishing himself as one of the competition’s most productive attackers.

#1330. Allegri: ‘Napoli’s Champions League fate is in our hands, but the league is more important’

Massimiliano Allegri insists Napoli’s Champions League fate is still in their own hands, but warned that turning their league form around matters more.

With quotes via TuttoMercatoWeb, the Napoli coach spoke at the Estádio do Dragão on Tuesday, before Wednesday’s game against Porto, which kicks off at 21:00 CET [20:00 GMT].

Allegri is back in the dugout after a two-match Serie A ban. During it, Napoli won 4-1 at Monza and lost 2-0 at Juventus, leaving them 10th on 14 points. In Europe, they have three points from three games after defeats in their first two matches and a 4-3 win over Bodø/Glimt.

He opened by paying tribute to Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel, who died at 30 after a collision with Andorra goalkeeper Owono during a match in Spain. “First of all, I’d like to offer my condolences to the family of Jesús de Miguel for this tragic accident to a young man, before a footballer, who lost his life,” he said.

“Tomorrow’s game is difficult, because Porto have won 10 in a row in the league, and they’ve played some good games in the Champions League too. As for us, talking is of little use, we need to put in a good performance. In the Champions League, our destiny is in our hands, because with 10 points we’d reach the play-offs at least. But then there’s the league to sort out, and that’s the most important thing.”

“Tomorrow isn’t the last chance. With 10 points you go to the play-offs. Tomorrow is an important game. Manchester is an important game but almost impossible. We’ll fight for qualification against Club Brugge, Viking and Sabah,” Allegri said.

He denied the injury crisis takes any pressure off. “It doesn’t take any pressure off, because it’s an important Champions League game against a strong team. Right now there’s no need to talk and explain. There’s only the need to act, to work, to get the injured players back and turn this negative period into a positive one.”

On Rasmus Højlund and Kevin De Bruyne, he said: “Højlund’s fever has gone. De Bruyne will train today, and afterwards we’ll see if he’s available for tomorrow.”

Asked about fears of a repeat of the season Napoli finished 10th, Allegri said: “Right now it’s time to act, not to talk. It’s not an easy moment. We’ve had mixed results and haven’t yet managed to win two league games in a row. But what’s certain is that we have to keep working, get back all the players who will return after the international break, and try to turn things around in the league, where there will be time and space to recover. In the meantime, we’re thinking about tomorrow, there’s a game to play.”

He returned Francesco Farioli’s praise. “I think Farioli, a young coach, has already achieved good results, both in the Netherlands and in Portugal. He has a very important career ahead of him.”

On the threat Porto pose at home: “We know Porto are very aggressive at home, and they have technical, physical and high-quality players. When we have the ball we’ll need to be good technically, and when we don’t we’ll need to defend well, which is something we’ve done less this season.”

Asked whether Porto would press with fewer players or match Napoli’s numbers, he said: “I don’t know, it depends on what Farioli decides. Whether it’s numbers even or an extra man, you have to behave in two completely different ways.”

#1328. Pocognoli backs returning star McTominay to lead Scotland into new era

Published: 15:09 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 15:55 EDT, 3 November 2026

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli has welcomed Scott McTominay back into the fold after heart surgery and revealed he’s banking on him to help kickstart a new era for the national team.

McTominay went through a minor operation to address mild benign arrhythmia in September and missed Pocognoli’s first Nations League camp as head coach.

However, having scored four times after returning to action at Italian outfit Napoli, the 29-year-old midfielder is back in the squad for this month’s double-header against North Macedonia and Switzerland.

Torino striker Che Adams, absent last time out due to a muscle strain, is also back in the fold while there is a first call-up for left-back James Penrice, currently on loan at Rangers from Greek side AEK Athens.

Celtic left-back Kieran Tierney returns after withdrawing from Pocognoli’s first squad while centre-back Scott McKenna misses out after reportedly picking up a back strain playing for Dinamo Zagreb. Josh Doig, Colby Donovan, James Wilson and Lennon Miller also drop out from Pocognoli’s debut matches.

Scott McTominay is fit and available for Scotland after minor heart surgery

Speaking while naming his squad at Hampden Park, Pocognoli emphasised the role McTominay will play – along with other senior stars – in helping bring through a new generation of stars under his guidance.

‘I have been in contact with Scott from the first day. He missed the first camp with some physical problem,’ stated the Belgian.

‘We were still in contact during the rehabilitation, when he came back on the pitch. He’s one of the captains, so there’s a special contact with them, but he’s looking forward to come, to play for us, to play in a different way, on the pitch and he is very positive, so that’s important.

‘There is plenty of experience back in the squad. With Scott, with Che, with Kieran. He’s also back, so, if you accumulate the caps, we have some experience that will be useful for this camp and to also embrace the young lads - because we still have a young squad with many players who don’t have a lot of caps.

‘I’m sure the mix will be good and these (experienced) players will also show the way for them.’

Sebastien Pocognoli has picked his squad to face North Macedonia and Switzerland

Scotland are third in Group B1 with four points from four games, three points behind Slovenia and eight behind runaway leaders Switzerland. The Scots host North Macedonia at Hampden on November 13 with a trip to Switzerland three days later.

With one eye on the forthcoming 2028 European Championship qualifying campaign, Pocognoli said: ‘I’m looking forward to working with everybody, but, for sure, we want to see most of the players just to have as much information as possible to start the qualification for the Euros.

‘All I want to do now is to get the most out of this, to know my squad as deeply as possible, to see the body language, the attitude of the players in some situations, and to have most of the information to start the big job.’

On the issue of a first call-up for 27-year-old former Hearts defender Penrice, Pocognoli said: ‘Like I said in the first camp, we have a list of players that we select regarding the performance at their clubs, but also the style of play or the way that we want to play.

‘We have some missing players around the left side, so, combined with his quality and what we are looking for on the pitch, it’s a logical choice for me. It can be very useful for the system that we want to play and also I think he deserves it.’

#1327. Politano: ‘Napoli are fragile at the moment, but no alibi against Porto’

Matteo Politano admits Napoli are ‘fragile’ defensively and concede too easily, but mustn’t ‘use injuries as an alibi’ for the Champions League trip to FC Porto.

It kicks off at the Estadio do Dragao on Wednesday at 20.00 GMT (21.00 CET).

The Partenopei are playing catch-up in the tournament after one win and two defeats, but that is still better than their opponents, who lost all three matches so far in the Champions League.

Max Allegri’s side also stumbled in Serie A at the weekend, losing 2-0 away to Juventus.

“A difficult game awaits us tomorrow. It’s true that we have some injuries, but this mustn’t be used as an alibi, we don’t want alibis at this moment,” said Politano in his press conference.

“We are the only ones who can drag ourselves out of this situation. We’ve got to give our all on the pitch, because this is a fundamental match for us.”

The recurring problem for Napoli this season is how many goals they are conceding, and assistant manager Marco Landucci confirmed players backing off when defending is not something suggested by the coaching staff.

“When we concede goals, it’s everyone’s fault and not just the defenders, this is a team sport,” confessed Politano.

“We are fragile at the moment, we can’t seem to defend as well as we did in previous years. We lack determination in pressing the opponents, so naturally against quality players you are going to pay for that.

“We’ve got to come together as a unit and try from tomorrow to be more solid. We haven’t tested the line-up yet, so we don’t know if it’ll be three or four at the back, but it is no problem for me.”

Napoli fumbled a lead for the 3-1 Champions League defeat to Villarreal, and Politano made a very costly error with a howler of a back-pass.

“Unfortunately, we can do nothing about the past, we need to focus on the future,” added the winger.

“I challenge myself every single day to give more, I’ve won a lot with this team, but I’ve got to keep pushing. It’s not an easy situation, we’ve all got to come together and stay concentrated at all times.

“Porto are a strong side, they attack in numbers and know how to keep the ball for long spells, so there are moments when we’ll be pinned back, waiting to then launch forward on the counter.

“It is fortunate that we have the opportunity so soon after the Juventus match to prove ourselves all over again, we were lacking something that we need to show tomorrow.”

#1325. Could a giant sunshade in space ‘solve global warming’? Scientists are taking the idea seriously

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Researchers say that a ‘planetary sunshade’ placed between Earth and the Sun could cool down the planet by 1 °C.Credit: Mongpro/Getty

In August, entrepreneur Elon Musk suggested in a social-media post that Earth could be cooled by launching satellites into space to shade the planet from the Sun. These “sentient satellites”, he wrote, “can solve global warming for ~1B years”.

Climate engineering faces hostility — here’s how scientists say it might move forwards

Climate engineering faces hostility — here’s how scientists say it might move forwards

It’s unclear whether Musk, chief executive of the aerospace firm SpaceX in Starbase, Texas, meant for this to be taken seriously. But some researchers are earnestly investigating space-based methods of reflecting sunlight away from Earth to cool the planet as temperatures rise to increasingly dangerous levels.

A non-profit organization called the Planetary Sunshade Institute in Los Angeles, California, published a report this month that researchers say is the most detailed analysis yet of such geoengineering methods. The report — which summarizes studies from a consortium of engineers and climate scientists, including some from leading space agencies such as NASA — estimates that it could become viable to begin building a ‘planetary sunshade’ in as few as 20–40 years. The timeline would depend on the rate at which heavy-lift rockets are developed that can haul millions of tonnes of material into deep space to create the sunshade. (SpaceX, which is not involved in the report, did not respond to a query from Nature about whether it is conducting research on this topic.)

A lot of people think this idea is “just fantasy”, says Chantal Cappelletti, a space-systems engineer at the University of Nottingham, UK, who is part of the consortium. But the falling cost of space launches have made the prospect seem more feasible, she says.

Blocking sunlight to cool the planet through solar geoengineering has long been controversial. Proposals have included releasing sunlight-reflecting particles into Earth’s atmosphere, which could affect the planet in poorly understood ways, such as disrupting precipitation and plant growth. Space-based approaches could come with unique risks, including the pollution unleashed from many thousands of rocket launches. Critics also say that focusing attention on geoengineering distracts from the urgent need to cut greenhouse-gas emissions to address climate change.

Controversial geoengineering projects to test Earth-cooling tech funded by UK agency

Controversial geoengineering projects to test Earth-cooling tech funded by UK agency

But solar geoengineering has received more attention from researchers as Earth looks set to hurtle past 1.5 °C of warming above the planet’s pre-industrial baseline temperature. The “accelerating climate crisis” is pushing the world towards solar geoengineering, says Morgan Goodwin, a climate activist and executive director of the Planetary Sunshade Institute.

The report is the group’s biggest project so far, funded by a £400,000 (US$530,000) grant from the UK Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA), a body sponsored by the government to fund high-risk, high-reward research. That grant is part of a larger £56.8-million ARIA research programme on solar geoengineering.

Daniele Visioni, a climate scientist at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, says that he had previously dismissed space-based approaches as science fiction. But after attending an engineering workshop on such approaches earlier this year, he was persuaded that they deserve more attention. However, “I still wouldn’t put this as something feasible before the end of the century”, he says.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03415-2

#1323. Oxlade-Chamberlain isn't the first big name to flop in Scotland... Five superstars who failed to make their mark in the Scottish top-flight

Published: 15:47 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 16:34 EDT, 3 November 2026

Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain's inability to nail down a starting slot in a struggling Celtic side has reinforced the theory that the hard and physical Scottish Premiership is not exactly a place for former English Premier League stars to head to in their twilight years with a view to coasting through to retirement.

Oxlade-Chamberlain arrived at Parkhead back in January with a sparkling CV that boasted a full house of domestic trophies in England plus a Champions League win and 35 international caps from spells at Southampton, Arsenal and Liverpool.

The 33-year-old has been unable to nail down a regular spot at Celtic Park, though, and was given a rare start at the weekend in the champions’ 2-0 loss away to Falkirk.

Here, in a Daily Mail Sport special, we look at five other big-name stars who have failed in Scotland in the wake of enjoying successful careers south of the border.

Arsenal legend Wright’s best days were long behind him when then Celtic manager John Barnes brought him in as a replacement for the injured Henrik Larsson up front during the 1999-2000 season.

Wright had been a sensation during his seven years at the Gunners, winning a full house of domestic trophies plus a European Cup-Winners’ Cup, but he’d been on loan at Nottingham Forest from West Ham before heading for Glasgow and was clearly over the hill at the age of 35.

He made 10 appearances in total during a short-lived spell that involved a 4-2 Old Firm loss and that infamous 3-1 Scottish Cup loss to Inverness Caledonian Thistle that led to Barnes’ departure.

Wright also left soon after for Burnley and admitted the entire affair left a mark.

He told the BBC: ‘I felt I was caught up in a war crisis in Kosovo not involved in a football result that wrecked John Barnes' career as Celtic manager.

'Some so-called fans, a few morons who know nothing better, covered my car in spit. They were shouting obscenities at myself and Regi Blinker.’

The former England midfielder had carved his reputation in the English Premier League during stays at Manchester City, Newcastle United and Queens Park Rangers and arrived at Rangers in September 2016 on a two-year deal after inspiring Burnley to promotion from the Championship.

His time in Glasgow, however, proved to be a short-lived train wreck. He left in the wake of having his contract cancelled after eight games and 133 days.

English midfielder Joey Barton did not impress in his short spell at Rangers

Barton arrived, aged 34, blowing his own trumpet and aiming verbal volleys at then Celtic’s Scott Brown, but his stay very quickly unravelled and involved a 5-1 Old Firm humbling in the east end of Glasgow in which he was targeted by the Parkhead midfielder.

In the aftermath, a training-ground bust-up involving Andy Halliday saw Barton told to stay away from Rangers by manager Mark Warburton and later hit with a three-week suspension.

It was the beginning of the end. His contract was cancelled in November.

The controversial Dane had earned a move to Spanish giants Real Madrid following five great years at Everton and arrived at Celtic from the Bernabeu on a three-year contract in August 2006 on a fee said to be in the region of £2million.

Gravesen did score a couple of goals against Rangers during his time in Glasgow, but never delivered the kind of performances required and failed to hold down a regular spot in the side by the end.

Thomas Gravesen was unimpressive at Celtic and clashed with manager Gordon Strachan

He played just 22 times before returning to Everton on a loan deal in August 2007. When the Goodison outfit refused to extend that arrangement, an agreement was struck to release him from his deal at Parkhead and he duly retired from playing.

Gravesen was hugely critical of then manager Gordon Strachan in later interviews.

‘Unfortunately, I ran into an opposition to myself in the form of a coach called Gordon Strachan. It did not work between him and me,’ he said.

‘Gordon was a defensively-minded coach of a world famous club. I could not understand why he did as he did at Celtic because we were so much better than the other teams. He was nervous about losing.’

The Welshman had won three FA Cups during a spell at Arsenal in addition to a Serie A title with Juventus when arriving on loan at Rangers from the Italian outfit in January 2022.

Rangers’ then sporting director Ross Wilson was quick to publicise his role in pulling the deal together and insisted it had sent a ripple of excitement through the dressing room at the Ibrox outfit.

However, Ramsey was unable to live up to expectations during the 13 appearances he made and was often battling fitness issues. He will be forever remembered for missing the decisive penalty-kick in the Europa League final shoot-out against Germans Eintracht Frankfurt in Seville after being sent on as a substitute by boss Giovanni van Bronckhorst late in extra-time.

Ramsey missed a penalty in Europa League final

Ramsey later told Four Four Two magazine: ‘I just wish that I’d played longer in the final. I felt I could have brought something different to the table had I come on a bit earlier.

‘I was essentially brought on solely to take a penalty in the shoot-out, which I’m not sure is the best idea. That played on my mind as I went to take it, instead of being clear about where I wanted to put it. I’m still gutted that I missed that penalty and gutted for the fans that we couldn’t lift the trophy for them.

'I was really excited to go to Rangers. I had a couple of injuries during my time there, which made it difficult to get into any kind of rhythm. I [also] had a horrible case of Covid shortly before I signed, which meant I didn’t arrive in the best shape and it was no surprise that my body broke down.’

The little midfielder had won the World Cup with Brazil before arriving at Celtic in 2004. He had become a legend at Middlesbrough, where he had three spells as a player.

He’d been the subject of a £13million move to Atletico Madrid following his first spell in England and there remains a theory that he never quite recovered from a broken leg suffered in Spain in a match against Celta Vigo.

Juninho actually started well at Parkhead by stepping into the heat of an Old Firm derby and delivering a fine display as Martin O’Neill’s side recorded a one-goal win.

Celtic fans did not see the best of Juninho

However, it quickly became clear he was a shadow of his former self and quickly slid onto the substitutes’ bench under O’Neill. By January, it had become clear he just wasn’t settling in and an agreement was made to release him from his contract after seven months and just 14 starts.

‘It was an awkward situation, and an especially frustrating one for me,’ recalled Juninho in later years.

‘I ended up in Scotland, but things didn’t really work out for me. I had this issue with Martin O’Neill and his tactics. I still can’t understand why he wanted me at Celtic. He used to play with a 4-4-2 and he asked me to play out wide with defensive responsibilities, but this was never my style. It didn’t suit me and he knew it.

‘Maybe inside his head, he wasn’t looking for the Juninho of the 90s and maybe I’m to blame for that, but a manager should know a player’s style.’

#1322. Carrick apology to United fans ominously similar to Solskjaer’s final match

There have been some dark days in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era but this was up there with the very worst of them: the kind of performance that gets a manager sacked, the kind of display that points to a fundamental disconnect, the kind of occasion that leaves you thinking Manchester United are as far away as they have ever been.

When players seem so averse to doing the very basics, such as running, and the club habitually have such trouble attracting the right profiles and personalities, it is hard to escape the feeling that saying goodbye to another manager is going to do little more than paper over the many cracks at Old Trafford.

But, watching this, you had to think Michael Carrick will do well to limp on as far as Sunday, when United face Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

And that was before we had heard the United captain, Bruno Fernandes, appearing to call out the manager’s tactics just a week on from the last show of public dissent from a player, when Lisandro Martínez attacked the Old Trafford board. If only these players were as good at talking on the pitch.

At the final whistle, Carrick walked over to the 700-strong group of United supporters, held up both hands in apology on no fewer than seven occasions and then walked off down the tunnel without looking in the direction of any of his players.

There were shades of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer at Watford in November 2021, when he also held up his hands in apology before being sacked 24 hours later.

In that instance, United fans booed Solskjaer. Carrick at least received some polite applause from the fans, who are a smart bunch and know the club’s problems extend far beyond the man in the dugout. Still, it is always the manager who pays the price. Solskjaer said he knew at half-time he was toast and Carrick is now under real threat himself – and seemingly at loggerheads with his captain.

Fernandes’s criticism of United’s set-up and approach was cutting and a direct attack on his manager and backroom team. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” the United captain said.

"I think sometimes we have to be more brave under pressure." Captain Bruno Fernandes gives his immediate reaction to Manchester United's heavy 4-1 defeat to Como 🗣️ 🎙️ @LiamMacdevitt 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/8bzmLGkRAX

There may be some truth in that, but Carrick’s response felt the most accurate assessment of the lot and will certainly chime with supporters who have long questioned how and why so many United sides, regardless of the manager, reach a point where running, intensity and urgency seem optional. “Whatever tactics you play, if you don’t run, and you don’t run forward, and you don’t run back, you ain’t going to win,” Carrick said.

Carrick has been telling us for weeks that he and his squad are together, that the team are not too far away, that it is all about small margins. He even described Sunday’s 1-1 draw at Leeds as a “fresh start”. But Como blew the lid off any pretence of that being the case. Even by the standards of this season to date, though, what unfolded here in the rain in Lombardy was shocking to witness.

Como, inspired by the outstanding Nico Paz, were every bit as good as United – who have won just two of 11 games this season – were a pitiful mess.

Having conceded after just 47 seconds to Atlético Madrid last week, United were behind after only 118 seconds this time. That in itself told you a lot about these players and this team and it set the tone for what was to follow: a masterclass in incompetence and indifference. There have only been four worse results in United’s European history, although you will struggle to find a poorer performance than this.

Paz scored the first and third goals and set up a wondrous second for Tasos Douvikas that showcased Como’s talent at the same time as underlining United’s myriad fault lines. Paz was just unplayable for much of an evening when United never got close to getting to grips with the young Argentine, whose big physique belies a bewitching ability on the ball. United, by contrast, were a sorry collection of strangers. It was impossible to discern a game plan. United were sent out in a strange 4-2-4, with Fernandes and Youri Tielemans operating as almost double false nines. Glenn Hoddle said on TNT Sports that it was like United were “playing in chains”.

Neither looked sure of what they were supposed to be doing. There was just a giant hole where the attack should have been. Everything about them was slow, leaden. The confusion was contagious. Everywhere you looked there were players second-guessing themselves, uncertain of their role and position and habitually a yard or two or three off the pace. But was there any excuse for not running, for so little effort?

The space Paz was afforded to curl in a fine finish less than two minutes in was alarming in the extreme. Carrick brought on Carlos Baleba and Amad Diallo for the lamentable Mateus Cunha and Andrey Santos at half-time, but United just got worse.

There was not so much as a snip at the heels of the same player when Paz ghosted in from the right flank, running 30 yards deep into the penalty area before again finishing coolly for the third. Ramón had a free header for the fourth.

As for that second shortly after the restart? First the impressive Lucas Da Cunha rolled Baleba too easily. Douvikas had positioned himself on Matthijs de Ligt’s blind side and the defender, making his first appearance for 11 months, had no idea where the Greece striker was before he darted across the front of him to receive Paz’s pass and dink the ball over Senne Lammens.

For Como, who were playing in Italy’s third tier five years ago, this was one of the greatest nights in their history. For United, it was one of the worst. Carrick may pay a heavy price for it, but there are far greater problems than the manager at this football club.

United enjoy a spell inside the attacking third to close the half, but it’s too late, at least for the first 45 minutes. The referee blows his whistle and we reach half-time with Como a goal to the good.

There are boos at half-time from United’s travelling support.

United send both of their full-backs forward and it gives Cunha the space to get a shot away from just outside of the box, but his curled effort sails over.

There will be one minute of time added on at the end of this half.

That’s a let off for United. Yan Couto, one of two former Manchester City signings in the Como team, carves open the United defence with a lovely pass and Douvikas should have done better with the finish.

Amazing the difference when you have a centre forward prepared to run in behind. Who would have thought it?

Baturina is the latest to threaten Lammens’ goal. His strike from the edge of the box stings the Belgian’s gloves and Douvikas, who attempts to latch on to the rebound, is offside.

Penalty shout for Como! Douvikas is sent through and it looks as though Lammens is in trouble as he sticks out a leg over which the Greek tumbles, but replays show Lammens withdraws his outstretched limb in the nick of time.

There was also an offside in the build-up, so it does not matter anyway.

Milla and Perrone are really pulling the strings in Como’s midfield. The former comes from the Jose Bordalas/Getafe school of football (think Tony Pulis during peak Britannia era) but you would not guess it given the way he manipulates the ball.

This game has entered into something of a holding pattern, with Como retaining possession as United chase shadows, desperately trying to lock off the centre of the park.

Here, Coute inverts, picking up the ball in the inside right channels before spinning in a ball over the top for Douvikas to stride on to, but the Greece forward shanks his shot over the bar.

Thirty four minutes in and the first chants of “attack, attack, attack” can be heard from the United fans. There is currently a giant hole where you would expect United’s strikers to be. It’s so poor.

Lammens does well to get down smartly and keep out a Douvikas effort, speared towards the near post after a sweeping counter attack. The resulting corner fails to threaten United’s defensive unit.

Da Cunha, fresh off his first France call-up, has just sold Mazraoui a dream, spinning the Moroccan in the middle of the pitch before gliding upfield, sweeping the ball out to Valle on the left, whose cross is far too loopy to trouble Lammens.

For seemingly the first time in this match, one of United’s full-backs, Mazraoui, makes a darting run in behind. While the ball goes through to the goalkeeper, it’s the right sort of intent.

Paz escapes the vicious clutches of Santos, but bumps into Cunha’s outstretched leg and earns a foul near the halfway line. Santos, already on a yellow, will need to careful not to get caught doing anything untoward for the remaining 60 minutes of this match.

It’s hard to detect a game plan from United. Como look like they know what what they’ve been told to do but United are just all over the place. Andrey Santos will be grateful referee Sven Jablonski was lenient the first time he came through the back of Paz because he’s just scythed through him a second time minutes later and picked up a yellow.

That’s better from United. Cunha hits the by-line aggressively but his cross is cut out.

Paz then breaks away down the right and, sensing a lack of cover, Santos dives in and receives a yellow card for his troubles.

United string together perhaps their best sequence of the match, shifting the ball quickly from one side to the other, with Mount and Cunha combining, but the move breaks down when Tielemans’ attempted through-ball is cut out by Kempf.

Fernandes attempts to play in Tielemans between the lines but his pass is behind the Belgian and Como regain possession. It’s rinse and repeat moments later, but on the far side.

The detail on United’s passes has been so poor thus far, with Como picking up loose balls all over the pitch.

Penalty shout for Como! Da Cunha, Douvikas and Baturina combine expertly through the middle, trading the ball with cultured one-touch passes. Baturina is felled by Maguire inside United’s box just as he was gearing up to shoot, but neither the referee nor the VAR are minded to intervene. There is a touch, but it does seem very slight.

United have gone with the box midfield once more, with Fernandes rolling inside as a false 9. Como are counteracting United’s movements through Paz dropping in, so Carrick’s men are struggling to take control of the central zones.

Mbeumo bursts towards the by-line but Ramon gets back sharply to divert the ball behind for a corner, which is easily dealt with.

United drop into a deep block, forcing Como to build around the outside. The ball is worked to the adventurous Couto who loses his boot after an overzealous challenge from Cunha and he earns a free-kick for his troubles, but Da Cunha’s delivery fails to beat the first man.

Chance! Da Cunha plays a lovely through-ball into the right channel for Paz to gallop on to and he flashes the ball across the face of goal, but Maguire gets there before Douvikas and the ball is cleared.

United are struggling to string passes together as Paz cuts out a Lammens pass out from the back, but he cannot keep the ball in play.

United need to settle, and here they decide it best to keep hold of the ball for a while. There are a few sideways passes but the ball goes back to Como.

Valle makes a burst down the left and Dalot’s contact results in a foul, but the free-kick is not up to much.

Como 1 Manchester United 0 (Paz) Well, we said he was special! Como work the ball out to the right, with Da Cunha picking out Paz on the edge of the box. Neither of United’s centre-halves are minded to close the Argentine down, and he opens up his body before shaping the ball around Lammens and inside the far post. Golazo.

Michael Carrick has insisted there is not a “toxic culture” at Manchester United in the wake of scathing criticism from former manager Erik ten Hag of the Old Trafford hierarchy and player power at the club.

The current United manager – who is under pressure after the club’s worst start to a season for 40 years – also believes he has the backing of the United board, despite Ten Hag accusing Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos regime of a series of “broken promises”.

In an interview with The Athletic, Ten Hag blamed Ratcliffe and his executives for fuelling a “toxic culture” by giving power to players and failing to back him on disciplinary matters relating to Marcus Rashford, Jadon Sancho and other first-teamers.

But Carrick said he had not encountered any toxicity since taking over from Ruben Amorim in January and suggested United’s last two outings, a 1-1 draw against Leeds United and a 2-0 defeat to Atlético Madrid, underlined the camaraderie in the group.

“Since I came back, the players and the staff have given us everything that they could give,” Carrick said before Wednesday’s Champions League clash against Cesc Fàbregas’s Como in northern Italy, where he is battling an injury and illness crisis.

“We’ve had some good performances. We’ve had some performances that we want to do better and we can improve on. We’ve made some mistakes.

Chelsea are reportedly interested in signing Everton midfielder Harrison Armstrong as Xabi Alonso looks to strengthen his options in the middle of the park ahead of the upcoming transfer windows.

According to Simon Phillips, the Blues have been closely monitoring the 19-year-old and are compiling regular scouting reports on his performances. Chelsea have also contacted his representatives in the past as they assess the possibility of bringing him to Stamford Bridge.

The England Under-21 international has established himself as one of Everton’s most promising young talents, making considerable progress since breaking into the senior squad.

His technical ability, composure in possession and versatility in midfield have attracted attention from several Premier League clubs. Armstrong has already made 32 senior appearances for Everton, providing four assists, and continues to develop into an important player for David Moyes.

Chelsea are looking to invest in young players with considerable potential, and Armstrong could be an exciting long-term addition. Alonso would benefit from having another technically gifted midfielder capable of providing energy and creativity in the centre of the pitch.

The Blues are also monitoring Newcastle United’s Lewis Miley, Fulham’s Josh King and Arsenal’s Myles Lewis-Skelly as they consider several options in midfield.

Phillips revealed on his YouTube channel: “Chelsea have looked at him in the last couple of windows, and they have actually made contact and spoke to his agents and stuff. So, this is a player that they are definitely very keen on – it’s Myles Lewis-Skelly from Arsenal. So, he is one of the players on this list, but he’s one that we have tracked before.

“The other three are completely new names.”

“Harrison Armstrong of Everton is another youngster that Chelsea are watching. 19 years old, central midfielder, playing quite a bit for Everton this season so far. Got a lot of clubs watching him.”

Phillips added: “The other two names is Josh King from Fulham – central midfielder, England Under-21 international. And then Lewis Miley from Newcastle – another England Under-21 international, plays in midfield, 6ft 2in tall.”

However, convincing Everton to part ways with their academy graduate will not be straightforward. The Toffees previously considered a £40 million offer from Nottingham Forest during the summer, but eventually abandoned the proposed transfer following a strong reaction from supporters.

Armstrong remains under contract at Everton until 2028, putting the Merseyside club in a reasonably strong negotiating position.

The club highly regards the midfielder, and there is little indication they would welcome another approach for his services.

Chelsea are expected to continue monitoring his development through regular scouting reports. Although the youngster fits their recruitment strategy, Everton’s determination to retain him could make negotiations extremely difficult.

#1320. Report Roma have lost Gollini for big Manchester United match

Bad news for Roma, as Pierluigi Gollini has not recovered from a back injury, so they are forced to choose a third-choice goalkeeper against Manchester United in the Champions League.

It kicks off at Old Trafford at 20.00 GMT (21.00 CEST).

There were concerns over the availability of Gollini for tonight’s game after he sustained a back problem during the last training session.

He would be given a late fitness test at the hotel in Manchester, but that proved negative, so Gollini is out of action for this huge fixture.

Gollini was already only filling in for first choice Mile Svilar, who has been out of action for over a month.

Sky Sport Italia, the Corriere dello Sport and more all confirm that the Italian is not available tonight at Old Trafford.

Now coach Gian Piero Gasperini must choose between two options for the third choice goalkeeper to make his season debut tonight.

Former Milan man Devis Vasquez is the favourite, though he was originally not even on the Champions League list, added on after Svilar’s injury.

The Colombian played one competitive match last season, for Besiktas against Karagumruk on April 27.

Another option is 19-year-old Giorgio De Marzi, who plays for the USA at Under-20 level.

There are also growing reports that Leonardo Balerdi and Rodrigo Mora will push into the starting XI for a very attack-minded formation, as Roma aim to make the most of a Manchester United team in crisis.

#1319. Former Spurs star Davinson Sanchez is embroiled in mass brawl during Galatasaray's Champions League clash vs Stuttgart - as an ex-Brighton striker is booked for his part in fracas

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 15:47 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 17:18 EDT, 3 November 2026

Davinson Sanchez found himself in the middle of an on-pitch brawl on Tuesday as he and his Galatasaray team-mates confronted their Stuttgart counterparts.

The incident came in the 37th minute of their 2-0 Champions League win over Stuttgart.

Looking to start a counter-attack from a Stuttgart corner, Galatasaray broke with Baris Yilmaz before his attempted pass was blocked out for a throw-in on the halfway line by Chris Fuhrich.

After shielding the ball out, Yilmaz reacted angrily to Fuhrich's pressure by dropping him to the ground in front of both dugouts.

That spat was then heightened when former Brighton striker Deniz Undav confronted Yilmaz in support of his Stuttgart team-mate Fuhrich.

That escalation saw the likes of former Tottenham defender Sanchez run over to get involved as players from both teams did likewise.

Former Tottenham defender Davinson Sanchez (centre left) was involved in a mass brawl between Galatasaray and Stuttgart players in the Champions League on Tuesday

Ex-Brighton striker Deniz Undav (right) was also involved as he defended his Stuttgart team

The incident was sparked after Chris Fuhrich (left) battled for the ball with Gala's Baris Yilmaz

Eventually once matters calmed down, Premier League referee Chris Kavanagh booked Yilmaz and Undav - with the likes of Fuhrich and Sanchez avoiding any sanctions.

And come full-time it was Yilmaz and Sanchez smiling as the hosts took the three points.

Aleksey Batrakov scored both goals in the opening 15 minutes of the match, with the second created after a lovely through-ball from Sanchez.

Gala have now won two and lost two of their opening four league phase matches, while this was Stuttgart's first defeat in the competition having won two of their previous games and drawing the other.

After this month's international break, Galatasaray then host Aston Villa on November 24, while Stuttgart travel to Inter Milan a day later.

#1318. The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

David Adam is a science journalist based near London.

You go to see a psychiatrist a decade from now. Alongside the usual questions about how you’re feeling, your work and your relationships, they look at biometric data from your phone about your sleep and speech patterns, examine the results of a blood test or a brain scan and even check your postcode to see whether your neighbourhood has high levels of pollution. An algorithm then compares that information with data from thousands of other people, determines which types of treatment have worked best for people similar to you and uses its findings to suggest a treatment regime.

How personalization and psychedelics are revitalizing psychiatry

How personalization and psychedelics are revitalizing psychiatry

That’s a vision of the future called precision psychiatry. And it’s a world away from most people’s experiences today. For all the progress that has been made across the medical sciences, psychiatry remains a frustratingly imprecise discipline. Doctors use someone’s symptoms and clinical history to make a diagnosis and prescribe treatments. But mental-health diagnoses are broad and can be vague — a particular therapy might transform one person’s life, but offer little help to someone else with apparently the same disorder.

As a result, people with mental-health conditions often find themselves cycling through treatments and doses, searching, mostly by trial and error, for one that works.

To improve things, psychiatrists want to divide broad diagnoses into more useful subgroups and match treatments to individuals using a data-driven approach. Some researchers are looking at genes and brain circuits; others are turning to data on speech, sleep or social circumstances. Psychiatrists working on The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), the discipline’s dominant classification system, are even considering how socio-economic, cultural and environmental factors might be incorporated in the future.

Why pharma firms are betting billions on psychedelic drugs despite setbacks

Why pharma firms are betting billions on psychedelic drugs despite setbacks

“I think precision psychiatry is certainly part of the future,” says Tom Insel, a psychiatrist and former director of the US National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), who now co-directs several mental-health-focused companies. “We’ll be able to say from the get-go, this patient needs this treatment and that’s where they’re going to do best.”

But some clinicians say that the personalized approach has yet to prove itself. Advances in genetics, brain imaging and biomarker research for psychiatry have failed to deliver on their promise before, and studies continue to reveal just how heterogeneous many psychiatric disorders are. “Psychiatry has this model that the white knight is going to ride over the hill and solve all our problems,” says Kenneth Kendler, a psychiatric geneticist at Virginia Commonwealth University in Richmond. “And we’ve been repeatedly disappointed.”

Personalized psychiatry is a catchy phrase, but it’s not a new idea.

Psychiatry has been trying to add precision to diagnosis and treatment for decades. In 1980, the third edition of the DSM introduced specific diagnostic criteria for many conditions. The aim was to boost reliability: a diagnosis of major depression or schizophrenia should mean roughly the same thing for everyone, even when issued by different psychiatrists.

But the DSM relies on symptoms to define conditions, and that proxy introduces complexities. The same symptoms appear in many conditions, and one person might have several diagnoses. Moreover, two people who have been diagnosed with the same condition can manifest it in quite different ways.

To meet DSM criteria for major depressive disorder, for example, a person must, in a two-week period, experience at least five symptoms out of a list of nine. The five must include a depressed mood or a loss of interest or pleasure; the remaining criteria include insomnia or excessive sleep, weight loss or gain, feelings of guilt or worthlessness and suicidal thoughts.

“It’s possible to have two people have the same diagnosis without a single required symptom in common,” says Vikram Patel, a psychiatrist at Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts.

Brain scans could help to stratify people with a condition such as depression into subtypes, or help psychiatrists to prescribe targeted treatments. Brain activity is lower in certain areas (red and yellow) in someone with untreated depression (top) than in someone who has received treatment.Credit: Wellcome Centre Human Neuroimaging/SPL

By the late 2000s, researchers were increasingly questioning whether the approved disease categories were the best way to classify and treat people.

At the NIMH, Insel helped to develop the Research Domain Criteria initiative, which tried to go beyond categories and instead study and measure processes such as reward, fear and cognition, which cut across diagnostic boundaries. The idea encouraged researchers to study behaviours and brain functions that are shared across conditions. Although the programme has helped to shift research towards the underlying mechanisms of illness, it was never intended to replace the symptoms-based diagnostic system, and it does not provide a reliable way to select treatments for individuals.

Another approach to precision is to measure someone’s symptoms and behaviour with more rigour. A psychiatrist assessing psychosis, for example, listens to a person and judges qualities such as coherence, paranoia and grandiosity. That relies on human expertise, but also introduces human subjectivity.

Insel imagines a machine-learning system listening to the same person speaking and assigning more objective, reproducible measurements. “The paranoia score here is 6.1,” he suggests. “The coherence level is 2.2.”

John Torous, a psychiatrist at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Centre in Boston and at Harvard Medical School, works on a related approach known as digital phenotyping, in which information from smartphones and wearable sensors is used to study behaviour. The term emerged around a decade ago, when researchers proposed that sensors already carried around in smartphones could provide continuous measures of various behaviours, such as physical mobility and communication, that could inform diagnosis1.

Can GLP-1s heal the brain? Obesity drugs get a makeover for addiction and depression

Can GLP-1s heal the brain? Obesity drugs get a makeover for addiction and depression

Small studies have since found links between activity levels and depressive and manic symptoms in bipolar disorder2, and between location data and symptom severity in schizophrenia3.

The difficulty has been turning these data into something that is useful in the clinic. Medical education has not generally trained clinicians to interpret this information, Torous says, and researchers have not yet developed standards and protocols for using it. “So, we are in the early days in that sense.”

Artificial intelligence could make the difference, he suggests, because it can analyse a range of data streams and package them into useful clinical information.

Digging into biology more deeply could offer another route to precision. As genetics and neuroscience continue to advance, some researchers hope that the insights they provide will help to separate broad psychiatric syndromes into distinct diseases, with different underlying biological mechanisms and, eventually, different treatments.

This hasn’t happened yet, and some argue that it’s a futile exercise. Whereas biological insights helped researchers to divide diabetes into two separate types nearly a century ago, “we’ve never approached that in psychiatry”, says Kendler. Mental-health conditions could be “heterogeneous a long way down”.

Still, genetics has managed to produce one of psychiatry’s more promising potential biomarkers. By looking at the genomes of thousands of people with schizophrenia, in a type of study called genome-wide association, researchers have gleaned some idea about which gene variants confer risk.

For most health conditions, it is the combined small effects of many variants that add up to susceptibility. Geneticists call this collective estimate of risk a polygenic risk score. People towards the top of the polygenic-risk distribution for schizophrenia, says Kendler, can have around a tenfold increase in risk, although the size of the relative increase varies depending on the study. Published estimates5, for example, put risk at about six times higher for the top 1% than for everyone else. But the scores cannot predict who will develop a condition.

“Is it at such a stage now that I would get that score and immediately change what I’m doing diagnostically? No,” Kendler says.

The hidden links between mental disorders

The hidden links between mental disorders

In five or ten years, he says, it is conceivable that a score distinguishing schizophrenia from bipolar disorder could help in a difficult case in which the distinction would affect treatment.

Researchers have also investigated levels of hormones and metabolites as psychiatric biomarkers. But Kendler says that such measures have “almost always” proved to be non-specific. An average biological difference between groups is hard to translate into a specific test that can flag what is wrong with a particular person, or which treatment to offer.

Brain imaging offers another version of the same problem. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies have reported large numbers of associations between features of the brain and psychiatric symptoms, but many of these have been difficult to reproduce.

A 2022 analysis6 of around 50,000 people found that associations between behavioural or mental-health traits and differences in brain structure or function were generally much smaller than previous studies had suggested.

Helen Mayberg, a neurologist at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City, says that scans can still provide clinically useful information if researchers ask specific-enough questions.

Prozac use for childhood depression skewed by single flawed medical trial

Prozac use for childhood depression skewed by single flawed medical trial

She has spent decades mapping brain circuits involved in depression, focusing on a region of the cortex called the subcallosal cingulate. This is tucked beneath the corpus callosum, the dense bundle of fibres that connects the two sides of the brain.

In one study7, researchers used functional MRI to scan the brains of 122 people with depression. They then assigned the individuals at random to one of two treatment groups: the first received 12 weeks of cognitive behavioural therapy, and the other received antidepressant medication for the same period of time.

The researchers found that connectivity between the subcallosal cingulate and three other brain regions differed according to the outcome of the treatment. People for whom psychotherapy worked and medication didn’t typically showed one pattern, whereas people with the opposite responses showed another.

In other words, this pattern of connectivity had the potential to act as a biomarker that can help assign treatment. “A scan done at baseline could actually help you to make that decision,” Mayberg says.

But there is a considerable distance between a potential biomarker and a routine clinical test. Mayberg says she has been told repeatedly that “nobody’s ever going to do a scan to decide how to treat people”, because it is too costly and time-consuming.

#1317. Official: Malagò vs. Galliani for FIGC President election on Dec 14

Giovanni Malagò has filed his candidacy for the fresh December 14 election as FIGC President and will be against former Milan and Monza chief Adriano Galliani.

Malagò of course had already won a landslide election in June, but that was declared null and void on October 6 because he did not have the right paperwork to run for the FIGC role.

He was instead given a new role as the FIGC special commissioner that same day, a way of providing continuity and in theory this was meant to tide him over until another election could be held, this time with the proper registration.

However, since then several parties who had backed his candidacy the first time have changed their minds, and are now supporting Galliani for the Presidency.

They include the Players’ Association and the Coaches’ Association, who have formally backed Galliani.

Today, Malagò formally filed his candidacy, co-signed by 11 Serie A clubs.

November 4 is the deadline for candidates, after which we can go into the new election on December 14.

Manchester United and Chelsea are reportedly interested in signing Como defender Jacobo Ramon as both clubs look to strengthen their defensive options ahead of next summer’s transfer window.

According to a report from Football Insider, the Premier League rivals have been impressed by the 21-year-old’s development in Italy. However, Real Madrid are currently in the strongest position to secure his services.

The Spanish defender has enjoyed an impressive rise since leaving Real Madrid for Como in 2025, establishing himself as an important member of Cesc Fabregas’ squad.

His performances have attracted considerable attention, with Manchester United viewing him as a potential long-term solution to their defensive problems. Chelsea are also monitoring his situation as they continue their strategy of recruiting promising young players with significant development potential.

This puts United and Chelsea at a significant disadvantage, with neither club likely to match the favourable conditions available to Real Madrid.

Both Premier League sides could continue monitoring his development, but their chances of securing his signature will depend heavily on the Spanish club’s intentions.

#1315. Champions League line-ups: Feyenoord vs. Inter

Inter badly need to revive their Champions League fortunes with a difficult trip to Feyenoord, as Francesco Pio Esposito, Federico Dimarco and Djed Spence start.

It kicks off at the Stadion De Kuip in Rotterdam at 20.00 GMT (21.00 CET).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from this game and Manchester United vs. Roma on the Liveblog.

The mood in the Nerazzurri camp is dismal after losing the Derby della Madonnina 3-1 to Milan at the weekend, their first Serie A defeat of the season which knocked them three points off leaders Lazio.

Their Champions League form had already been raising eyebrows, losing the first two fixtures to Real Madrid and Club Brugge, then scraping a 1-0 victory over Shakhtar Donetsk when down to 10 men.

Alessandro Bastoni was sent off in that game and is therefore suspended here, with Lautaro Martinez, Curtis Jones, Luis Henrique and John Stones still injured.

Choices were very limited in the derby because of a flu bug sweeping through the squad, but Pio Esposito has recovered and is able to start with Marcus Thuram.

Dimarco and Piotr Zielinski also return to the starting XI, while Benjamin Pavard is at least an option off the bench now.

Spence keeps the right wing-back role, with Hakan Calhanoglu and Nicolò Barella in midfield.

Feyenoord have already beaten Como here in the Champions League, confirming they are a very different side on home turf.

They have quite a few injuries to deal with this evening, missing Jakub Moder, Bart Nieuwkoop, Gijs Smal, Jeremiah St. Juste, Thomas Beelen and Jordan Bos.

Anis Hadj Moussa was very impressive in the game against Como, and is certainly one to watch attacking Dimarco down that flank.

These teams faced off in the Champions League Round of 16 last season, Inter winning 2-0 away and 2-1 at San Siro.

Feyenoord: Ernst; Read, Kraaijeveld, Marmol, Javi Lopez; Zechiel, Vanhoutte, Targhalline; Hadj Moussa, Ferri, Valente

Inter: J Martinez; Bisseck, Akanji, Carlos Augusto; Spence, Barella, Calhanoglu, Zielinski, Dimarco; Thuram, Esposito

Inter bench: Di Gennaro, Provedel, Stankovic, Sucic, Bonny, Diouf, Mkhitaryan, Pavard, Stante, Bovio, Mosconi, Lavelli

Liverpool are reportedly in a strong position to sign Monaco midfielder Lamine Camara as Andoni Iraola looks to strengthen his midfield options during the January transfer window.

According to a report from Football Insider, Monaco are now willing to negotiate a potential departure for the Senegal international, while the player is also open to discussing a move to Anfield. The Reds have maintained their interest after monitoring his situation throughout the summer.

The 22-year-old has established himself as one of the most promising young midfielders in French football, attracting attention with his energy, technical ability and impressive performances for Monaco.

Liverpool are keen to add another quality central midfielder to their squad, and Camara could provide greater balance and dynamism in the middle of the park. His ability to contribute defensively while also progressing the ball would make him an attractive option for Iraola.

The Senegalese international came close to joining Chelsea during the summer transfer window, with the Blues reportedly agreeing a deal worth £47 million. However, Monaco eventually pulled out of the negotiations after another proposed departure from their squad failed to materialise.

Chelsea have now shifted their attention towards alternative midfield targets, potentially leaving Liverpool in a favourable position to complete the transfer.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

However, Liverpool will still need to negotiate an agreement with the French club. Monaco are reportedly looking for a fee in the region of £50 million to sanction his departure in January.

The Ligue 1 side are keen to generate significant funds after failing to offload Camara during the previous transfer window. Their financial situation could therefore work in Liverpool’s favour.

The midfielder has also remained an important member of the squad, featuring consistently in Ligue 1 this season and demonstrating his importance to the team.

Liverpool are expected to continue discussions over a potential move, with January offering an opportunity to secure one of their long-term midfield targets. Although negotiations could still prove complicated, the Reds appear well placed to make progress in the transfer race.

#1312. Aston Villa 2.0 are making mockery of the early-season doom merchants

Two months ago there were many doom merchants insisting that Aston Villa were heading for a season of struggle, but they are looking foolish now.

After a summer of uncertainty and much change, Villa are stepping into a brave new era and find themselves joint-top of the Champions League table after three matches.

With co-owner Nassef Sawiris in attendance, Villa fans are dreaming of another magical season almost four years after Emery walked through the doors at this historic club.

Sawiris was the key figure driving Emery’s appointment in October 2022 and few could have predicted the success that has followed with the Basque manager at the helm.

Villa 2.0 have made a flawless start to their European campaign and are running into form in the Premier League after a sticky start.

In this comfortable victory over Viking, Villa became the second fastest team to win 20 matches at this level from 30 matches, only behind Real Madrid (who won 20 of their first 29). They have also won 12 home games in Europe in a row.

Much tougher assignments are to come, with powerhouses Barcelona, Paris St-Germain and Borussia Dortmund still to come in the league phase.

Yet Villa are currently level on points with Paris St-Germain, Liverpool and Real Madrid, and Emery remains determined to make an impact in this competition.

He said: “We are delighted with how we are responding and improving things. The Champions League is very difficult, but we have nine points and you can feel confidence. We are comfortable for the next challenge.”

What a difference a few months make. Over the course of the summer, many observers wondered if the Emery fairy tale was in danger of ending.

With six of the starting XI from last season’s Europa League final victory moving on, it could have been a difficult period of transition. We have all learnt, however, that Emery can never be written off or doubted.

Just a week after their biggest European win, the 6-0 destruction of Fenerbahce, expectations were understandably high. Before kick-off a huge tifo was unfurled in the Holte End with the words: “We’ve conquered before. We’re prepared for more.”

This was not as comfortable but still an impressive performance from this new and exciting team. Alysson, the Brazilian winger, was their man of the match.

Emery had warned his players of complacency against the Norwegian champions, but Villa took command from the start and were ahead after 23 minutes.

Ross Barkley scored twice against Fenerbahce last week and was in the right place again to head Ibrahim Mbaye’s corner past Arild Ostbo.

Hopes of another famous European night here never appeared likely, even though their 2,500 travelling supporters remained noisy all evening.

A first win of the campaign tonight would represent another huge shock.

Sawiris was the main driver behind the appointment of Unai Emery almost four years ago. Worked out ok, hasn’t it?

Elsewhere in Europe this evening, Manchester United are currently 4-0 down against Cesc Fabregas’ Como. Nico Paz has starred with two goals and an assist. Could this spell the end of Michael Carrick’s tenure in charge of Man Utd? You can keep up with the action and post-match reaction here.

Speaking to the club’s official website in his match preview, the Aston Villa boss said: “Champions League, every team they are playing Champions League, they are because they deserve it and they are dangerous and they have their collective and individual issues or characteristics as a team.

“Viking, they drew against Bayern Munich last week, they lost against Stuttgart. They are with Bodø/Glimt in the league, first and second with the same points.

“Bodø/Glimt is a team successful the last years in Europe, performing well, getting good results, playing Champions League, beating important teams.

“So Viking now is a new team as well, with the with the capacity to draw against Bayern Munich, the capacity as well to compete against Stuttgart and to compete against us tomorrow.

“This is Champions League, and Champions League is very difficult. In Champions League, we have now six points, it’s something amazing, but very difficult, and to keep the same way we are is our challenge.

“It’s not only Champions League, because Europa League is very difficult, and Conference League is very difficult. Europe is always very difficult.

“This is the first respect. We are Champions League, and each team is, of course, very, very respectful for us.”

Ibrahim Mbaye has slowly been embedded into the first team picture at Aston Villa by Unai Emery following his big money to England in the summer. #1309. Dengue comes back even in vaccinated people — new clues

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

People who are infected with dengue virus for a second time often develop severe disease.Credit: Mamunur Rashid/NurPhoto via Getty

Infecting people with a weak strain of dengue virus is helping researchers to unravel the disease’s bizarre effects on the immune system.

Dengue is spread when someone is bitten by an infected female Aedes mosquito. The viral disease kills around 40,000 people every year, with up to 400 million infected annually. Bangladesh and Kenya are among the countries battling a deadly outbreak. Although most adults survive their first brush with the disease, people who are exposed to a second, different strain of dengue virus often develop more severe symptoms.

This unusual quirk has complicated dengue vaccine development. Now, a human challenge trial that exposed 45 people to a modified mild strain of dengue virus is beginning to reveal the immunological underpinnings of dengue’s second wind, according to a study published in Science Translational Medicine on 28 October1.

Understanding the biology behind dengue’s infection pattern could help researchers to develop better vaccines, says study co-author Leah Katzelnick, an epidemiologist at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases in Bethesda, Maryland.

“Dengue is still considered a neglected tropical disease,” she says. “But it’s become a problem for almost everyone now.”

Part of the problem with existing dengue vaccines is that even the immunizations can trigger secondary infections. This issue caused concern in the Philippines when some children contracted severe dengue infections after a major public vaccination effort started there in 2016.

Why the secondary infections happen is unclear. One theory is that, when confronted with a different dengue virus strain, the immune system deploys antibodies that were originally generated against the previous dengue strain it encountered. These antibodies aren’t as effective against the second strain, which can lead to people experiencing worse symptoms. Subsequent infections with other variants of dengue don’t seem to trigger the same immune response.

To learn more about how dengue immunology works, Katzelnick and her colleagues recruited 45 healthy people and split them into three groups: those who had never been infected with dengue; others who had been infected by one dengue virus strain; and those who had been infected by several dengue strains. The team then exposed all participants to a weakened version of DENV-3 (one of four strains of the virus) and compared their immune responses using blood and lymph-node samples.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03488-z

Odio, C. D. et al. Sci. Transl. Med. 18, eaei5117 (2026).
